entries.source: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv21"/><title type="x-ms">Ezra</title> <div sID="gen8522" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8523" type="x-p"/> The Jewish church puts on quite another face in this book from what it had appeared with; its state much better, and more pleasant, than it was of late in Babylon, and yet far inferior to what it had been formerly. The dry bones here live again, but <hi type="italic">in the form of a servant;</hi> the yoke of their captivity is taken off, but the marks of it in their galled necks remain. Kings we hear no more of; <hi type="italic">the crown has fallen from their heads.</hi> Prophets they are blessed with, to direct them in their re-establishment, but, after a while, prophecy ceases among them, till the great prophet appears, and his fore-runner. The history of this book is the accomplishment of Jeremiah's prophecy concerning the return of the Jews out of Babylon at the end of seventy years, and a type of the accomplishment of the prophecies of the Apocalypse concerning the deliverance of the gospel church out of the New-Testament Babylon. Ezra preserved the records of that great revolution and transmitted them to the church in this book. His name signifies a helper; and so he was to that people. A particular account concerning him we shall meet with, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.1-Ezra.7.28">ch. vii.</reference>, where he himself enters upon the stage of action. The book gives us an account, I. Of the Jews' return out of their captivity, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.1-Ezra.2.70">ch. i., ii.</reference> II. Of the building of the temple, the opposition it met with, and yet the perfecting of it at last, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.1-Ezra.6.22">ch. iii.-vi.</reference> III. Of Ezra's coming to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.1-Ezra.8.36">ch. vii., viii.</reference> IV. Of the good service he did there, in obliging those that had married strange wives to put them away, <reference osisRef="Ezra.9.1-Ezra.10.44">ch. ix., x.</reference> This beginning again of the Jewish nation was small, yet its latter end greatly increased. <div eID="gen8523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8524" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8525" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The proclamation which Cyrus, king of Persia, issued out for the release of all the Jews that he found captives in Babylon, and the building of their temple in Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.1-Ezra.1.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. The return of many thereupon, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.5-Ezra.1.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. III. Orders given for the restoring of the vessels of the temple, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.7-Ezra.1.11">ver. 7-11</reference>. And this is the dawning of the day of their deliverance. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv21"/> <div eID="gen8525" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8524" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Proclamation of Cyrus. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 536.)</title> <div sID="gen8526" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now in the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> by the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia, that he made a proclamation throughout all his kingdom, and <hi type="italic">put it</hi> also in writing, saying, <hi type="super">2</hi> Thus saith Cyrus king of Persia, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of heaven hath given me all the kingdoms of the earth; and he hath charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Judah. <hi type="super">3</hi> Who <hi type="italic">is there</hi> among you of all his people? his God be with him, and let him go up to Jerusalem, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Judah, and build the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, (he <hi type="italic">is</hi> the God,) which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">4</hi> And whosoever remaineth in any place where he sojourneth, let the men of his place help him with silver, and with gold, and with goods, and with beasts, beside the freewill offering for the house of God that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Jerusalem. <div eID="gen8526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8527" type="x-p"/> It will be proper for us here to consider, 1. What was the state of the captive Jews in Babylon. It was upon many accounts very deplorable; they were under the power of those that hated them, had nothing they could call their own; they had no temple, no altar; if they sang psalms, their enemies ridiculed them; and yet they had prophets among them. Ezekiel and Daniel were kept distinct from the heathen. Some of them were preferred at court, others had comfortable settlements in the country, and they were all borne up with hope that, in due time, they should return to their own land again, in expectation of which they preserved among them the distinction of their families, the knowledge of their religion, and an aversion to idolatry. 2. What was the state of the government under which they were. Nebuchadnezzar carried many of them into captivity in the first year of his reign, which was the fourth of Jehoiakim; he reigned forty-five years, his son Evil-merodach twenty-three, and his grandson Belshazzar three years, which make up the seventy years. So Dr. Lightfoot, It is charged upon Nebuchadnezzar that he <hi type="italic">opened not the house of his prisoners,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.14.17">Isa. xiv. 17</reference>. And, if he had shown mercy to the poor Jews, Daniel told him it would have been the <hi type="italic">lengthening of his tranquillity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.4.27">Dan. iv. 27</reference>. But the measure of the sins of Babylon was at length full, and then destruction was brought upon them by Darius the Mede and Cyrus the Persian, which we read of, <reference osisRef="Dan.5.31">Dan. v.</reference> Darius, being old, left the government to Cyrus, and he was employed as the instrument of the Jews' deliverance, which he gave orders for as soon as ever he was master of the kingdom of Babylon, perhaps in contradiction to Nebuchadnezzar, whose family he had cut off, and because he took a pleasure in undoing what he had done, or in policy, to recommend his newly-acquired dominion as merciful and gentle, or (as some think) in a pious regard to the prophecy of Isaiah, which had been published, and well known, above 150 years before, where he was expressly named as the man that should do this for God, and for whom God would do great things (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Isa. xliv. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.45.1">xlv. 1</reference>, &c.), and which perhaps was shown to him by those about him. His name (some say) in the Persian language signifies the <hi type="italic">sun,</hi> for he brought light and healing to the church of God, and was an eminent type of Christ the <hi type="italic">Sun of righteousness.</hi> Some was that his name signifies a <hi type="italic">father,</hi> and Christ is the everlasting Father. Now here we are told, <div eID="gen8527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8528" type="x-p"/> I. Whence this proclamation took its rise. <hi type="italic">The Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus.</hi> Note, The hearts of kings are in the hand of the Lord, and, like the rivulets of water, he turneth them which way soever he will. It is said of Cyrus that he knew not God, nor how to serve him; but God knew him, and how to serve himself by him, <reference osisRef="Isa.45.4">Isa. xlv. 4</reference>. God governs the world by his influence on the spirits of men, and, whatever good is done at any time, it is God that stirs up the spirit to do it, puts thoughts into the mind, gives to the understanding to form a right judgment, and directs the will which way he pleases. Whatever good offices therefore are, at any time, done for the church of God, he must have the glory of them. <div eID="gen8528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8529" type="x-p"/> II. The reference it had to the prophecy of Jeremiah, by whom God had not only promised that they should return, but had fixed the time, which set time to favour Sion had now come. Seventy years were determined (<reference osisRef="Jer.25.12">Jer. xxv. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.29.10">xxix. 10</reference>); and he that kept the promise made concerning Israel's deliverance out of <hi type="italic">Egypt to a day</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">Exod. xii. 41</reference>) was doubtless as punctual to this. What Cyrus now did was long since said to be the <hi type="italic">confirming of the word of God's servants,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.44.26">Isa. xliv. 26</reference>. Jeremiah, while he lived, was hated and despised; yet thus did Providence honour him long after, that a mighty monarch was influenced to act in pursuance of the word of the Lord by his mouth. <div eID="gen8529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8530" type="x-p"/> III. The date of this proclamation. It was in his first year, not the first of his reign over Persia, the kingdom he was born to, but the first of his reign over Babylon, the kingdom he had conquered. Those are much honoured whose spirits are stirred up to begin with God and to serve him in their first years. <div eID="gen8530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8531" type="x-p"/> IV. The publication of it, both by word of mouth (he <hi type="italic">caused a voice to pass throughout all his kingdom,</hi> like a jubilee-trumpet, a joyful sabbatical year after many melancholy ones, proclaiming liberty to the captives), and also in black and white: he put it in writing, that it might be the more satisfactory, and might be sent to those distant provinces where the ten tribes were scattered in Assyria and Media, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.6">2 Kings xvii. 6</reference>. <div eID="gen8531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8532" type="x-p"/> V. The purport of this proclamation of liberty. <div eID="gen8532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8533" type="x-p"/> 1. The preamble shows the causes and considerations by which he was influenced, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.2">v. 2</reference>. It should seem, his mind was enlightened with the knowledge of <hi type="italic">Jehovah</hi> (for so he calls him), the God of Israel, as the only <hi type="italic">living and true God,</hi> the <hi type="italic">God of heaven,</hi> who is the sovereign Lord and disposer of all <hi type="italic">the kingdoms of the earth;</hi> of him he says <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.3">(v. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">He is the God,</hi> God alone, God above all. Though he had not known God by education, God made him so far to know him now as that he did this service with an eye to him. He professes that he does it, (1.) In gratitude to God for the favours he had bestowed upon him: <hi type="italic">The God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth.</hi> This sounds a little vain-glorious, for there were <hi type="italic">many kingdoms of the earth</hi> which he had nothing to do with; but he means that God had given him all that was given to Nebuchadnezzar, whose dominion, Daniel says, was <hi type="italic">to the end of the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.4.22">Dan. iv. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.5.19">v. 19</reference>. Note, God is the fountain of power; the kingdoms of the earth are at his disposal; whatever share any have of them they have from him: and those whom God has entrusted with great power and large possessions should look upon themselves as obliged thereby to do much for him. (2.) In obedience to God. He hat <hi type="italic">charged me to build him a house at Jerusalem;</hi> probably by a dream or vision of the night, confirmed by comparing it with the prophecy of Isaiah, where his doing it was foretold. Israel's disobedience to God's charge, which they were often told of, is aggravated by the obedience of this heathen king. <div eID="gen8533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8534" type="x-p"/> 2. He gives free leave to all the Jews that were in his dominions to go up to Jerusalem, and to <hi type="italic">build the temple of the Lord</hi> there, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.3">v. 3</reference>. His regard to God made him overlook, (1.) The secular interest of his government. It would have been his policy to keep so great a number of serviceable men in his dominions, and seemed impolitic to let them go and take root again in their own land; but piety is the best policy. (2.) The honour of the religion of his country. Why did he not order them to build a temple to the gods of Babylon or Persia? He believed the God of Israel to be the <hi type="italic">God of heaven,</hi> and therefore obliged his Israel to worship him only. Let them <hi type="italic">walk in the name of the Lord their God.</hi> <div eID="gen8534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8535" type="x-p"/> 3. He subjoins a brief for a collection to bear the charges of such as were poor and not able to bear their own, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.4">v. 4</reference>. "Whosoever remaineth, because he has not the means to bear his charges to Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">let the men of his place help him.</hi>" Some take it as an order to the king's officers to supply them out of his revenue, as <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.8">ch. vi. 8</reference>. But it may mean a warrant to the captives to ask and receive the alms and charitable contributions of all the king's loving subjects. And we may suppose the Jews had conducted themselves so well among their neighbours that they would be as forward to accommodate them because they loved them as the Egyptians were because they were weary of them. At least many would be kind to them because they saw the government would take it well. Cyrus not only gave his good wishes with those that went (<hi type="italic">Their God be with them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.3">v. 3</reference>), but took care also to furnish them with such things as they needed. He took it for granted that those among them who were of ability would offer their <hi type="italic">free-will offerings for the house of God,</hi> to promote the rebuilding of it. But, besides that, he would have them supplied out of his kingdom. Well-wishers to the temple should be well-doers for it.

<div eID="gen8535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8536" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Then rose up the chief of the fathers of Judah and Benjamin, and the priests, and the Levites, with all <hi type="italic">them</hi> whose spirit God had raised, to go up to build the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">6</hi> And all they that <hi type="italic">were</hi> about them strengthened their hands with vessels of silver, with gold, with goods, and with beasts, and with precious things, beside all <hi type="italic">that</hi> was willingly offered. <hi type="super">7</hi> Also Cyrus the king brought forth the vessels of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , which Nebuchadnezzar had brought forth out of Jerusalem, and had put them in the house of his gods; <hi type="super">8</hi> Even those did Cyrus king of Persia bring forth by the hand of Mithredath the treasurer, and numbered them unto Sheshbazzar, the prince of Judah. <hi type="super">9</hi> And this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the number of them: thirty chargers of gold, a thousand chargers of silver, nine and twenty knives, <hi type="super">10</hi> Thirty basons of gold, silver basons of a second <hi type="italic">sort</hi> four hundred and ten, <hi type="italic">and</hi> other vessels a thousand. <hi type="super">11</hi> All the vessels of gold and of silver <hi type="italic">were</hi> five thousand and four hundred. All <hi type="italic">these</hi> did Sheshbazzar bring up with <hi type="italic">them of</hi> the captivity that were brought up from Babylon unto Jerusalem. <div eID="gen8536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8537" type="x-p"/> We are here told, <div eID="gen8537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8538" type="x-p"/> I. How Cyrus's proclamation succeeded with others. 1. He having given leave to the Jews to go up to Jerusalem, many of them went up accordingly, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.5">v. 5</reference>. The leaders herein were the <hi type="italic">chief of the fathers</hi> of Judah and Benjamin, eminent and experienced men, from whom it might justly be expected that, as they were above their brethren in dignity, so they should go before them in duty. The priests and Levites were (as became them) with the first that set their faces again towards Zion. If any good work is to be done, let ministers lead in it. Those that accompanied them were such as God had inclined to go up. The same God that had raised up the spirit of Cyrus to proclaim this liberty raised up their spirits to take the benefit of it; for it was done, <hi type="italic">not by might, nor by power, but by the Spirit of the Lord of hosts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.4.6">Zech. iv. 6</reference>. The temptation perhaps was strong to some of them to stay in Babylon. They had convenient settlements there, had contracted an agreeable acquaintance with the neighbours, and were ready to say, <hi type="italic">It is good to be here.</hi> The discouragements of their return were many and great, the journey long, their wives and children unfit for travelling, their own land was to them a strange land, the road to it an unknown road. Go up to Jerusalem! And what should they do there? It was all in ruins, and in the midst of enemies to whom they would be an easy prey. Many were wrought upon by these considerations to stay in Babylon, at least not to go with the first. But there were some that got over these difficulties, that ventured to break the ice, and feared not the lion in the way, the lion in the streets; and they were those whose spirits God raised. He, by his Spirit and grace, filled them with a generous ambition of liberty, a gracious affection to their own land, and a desire of the free and public exercise of their religion. Had God left them to themselves, and to the counsels of flesh and blood, they would have staid in Babylon; but he put it into their hearts to set their faces Zionward, and, as strangers, to ask the way thither (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.5">Jer. l. 5</reference>); for they, being a new generation, went out like their father Abraham from this land of the Chaldees, not knowing whither they went, <reference osisRef="Heb.11.8">Heb. xi. 8</reference>. Note, Whatever good we do, it is owing purely to the grace of God, and he raises up our spirits to the doing of it, <hi type="italic">works in us both to will and to do.</hi> Our spirits naturally incline to this earth and to the things of it. If they move upwards, in any good affections or good actions, it is God that raises them. The call and offer of the gospel are like Cyrus's proclamation. <hi type="italic">Deliverance is preached to the captives,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.4.18">Luke iv. 18</reference>. Those that are bound under the unrighteous dominion of sin, and bound over to the righteous judgment of God, may be made free by Jesus Christ. Whoever will, by repentance and faith, return to God, his duty to God, his happiness in God, Jesus Christ has opened the way for him, and let him go up out of the slavery of sin into the <hi type="italic">glorious liberty of the children of God.</hi> The offer is general to all. Christ makes it, in pursuance of the grant which the Father has made him of <hi type="italic">all power both in heaven and in earth</hi> (a much greater dominion than that given to Cyrus, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.2">v. 2</reference>) and of the charge given him to <hi type="italic">build God a house,</hi> to set him up a church in the world, a kingdom among men. Many that hear this joyful sound choose to sit still in Babylon, are in love with their sins and will not venture upon the difficulties of a holy life; but some there are that break through the discouragements, and resolve to <hi type="italic">build the house of God,</hi> to make heaven of their religion, whatever it cost them, and they are those <hi type="italic">whose spirit God has raised</hi> above the world and the flesh and whom he has made <hi type="italic">willing in the day of his power,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. Thus will the heavenly Canaan be replenished, though many perish in Babylon; and the gospel-offer will not be made in vain. 2. Cyrus having given order that their neighbours should help them, they did so, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.6">v. 6</reference>. All those that were about them furnished them with plate and goods to bear the charges of their journey, and to help them in building and furnishing both their own houses and God's temple. As the tabernacle was made of the spoils of Egypt, and the first temple built by the labours of the strangers, so the second by the contributions of the Chaldeans, all intimating the admission of the Gentiles into the church in due time. God can, where he pleases, incline the hearts of strangers to be kind to his people, and make those to strengthen their hands that have weakened them. <hi type="italic">The earth helped the woman. Besides what was willingly offered</hi> by the Jews themselves who staid behind, from a principle of love to God and his house, much was offered, as one may say, unwillingly by the Babylonians, who were influenced to do it by a divine power on their minds of which they themselves could give no account. <div eID="gen8538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8539" type="x-p"/> How this proclamation was seconded by Cyrus himself. To give proof of the sincerity of his affection to the house of God, he not only released the people of God, but restored the vessels of the temple, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.7-Ezra.1.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Observe here, 1. How careful Providence was of the vessels of the temple, that they were not lost, melted down, or so mixed with other vessels that they could not be known, but that they were all now forthcoming. Such care God has of the living <hi type="italic">vessels of mercy, vessels of honour,</hi> of whom it is said (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19-2Tim.2.20">2 Tim. ii. 19, 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">The Lord knows those that are his,</hi> and they shall <hi type="italic">none of them perish.</hi> 2. Though they had been put into an idol's temple, and probably used in the service of idols, yet they were given back, to be used for God. God will recover his own; and the spoil of the strong man armed shall be converted to the use of the conqueror. 3. Judah had a prince, even in captivity. Sheshbazzar, supposed to be the same with Zerubbabel, is here called <hi type="italic">prince of Judah;</hi> the Chaldeans called him <hi type="italic">Sheshbazzar,</hi> which signifies <hi type="italic">joy in tribulation;</hi> but among his own people he went by the name of <hi type="italic">Zerubbabel—a stranger in Babylon;</hi> so he looked upon himself, and considered Jerusalem his home, though, as Josephus says, he was captain of the life-guard to the king of Babylon. He took care of the affairs of the Jews, and had some authority over them, probably from the death of Jehoiachin, or Jeconiah, who made him his heir, he being of the house of David. 4. To him the sacred vessels were numbered out (<reference osisRef="Ezra.1.8">v. 8</reference>), and he took care for their safe conveyance to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Ezra.1.11">v. 11</reference>. It would encourage them to build the temple that they had so much rich furniture ready to put into it when it was built. Though God's ordinances, like the vessels of the sanctuary, may be corrupted and profaned by the New-Testament Babylon, they shall, in due time, be restored to their primitive use and intention; for not one jot or tittle of divine institution shall fall to the ground.  <chapter eID="Ezra.1"/> <div eID="gen8539" type="x-p"/>

<div sID="gen8544" type="x-p"/> We may observe here, 1. That an account was kept in writing of the families that came up out of captivity, and the numbers of each family. This was done for their honour, as part of their recompence for their faith and courage, their confidence in God and their affection to their own land, and to stir up others to follow their good example. Those that honour God he will thus honour. The names of all those Israelites indeed that accept the offer of deliverance by Christ shall be found, to their honour, in a more sacred record than this, even in <hi type="italic">the Lamb's book of life.</hi> The account that was kept of the families that came up from the captivity was intended also for the benefit of posterity, that they might know from whom they descended and to whom they were allied. 2. That they are called <hi type="italic">children of the province.</hi> Judah, which had been an illustrious kingdom, to which other kingdoms had been made provinces, subject to it and dependent on it, was now itself made a province, to receive laws and commissions from the king of Persia and to be accountable to him. See how sin diminishes and debases a nation, which righteousness would exalt. But by thus being made servants (as the patriarchs by being sojourners in a country which was theirs by promise) they were reminded of the <hi type="italic">better country, that is, the heavenly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.11.16">Heb. xi. 16</reference>), a <hi type="italic">kingdom which cannot be moved,</hi> or changed into a province. 3. That they are said to come <hi type="italic">every one to his city,</hi> that is, the city appointed them, in which appointment an eye, no doubt, was had to their former settlement by Joshua; and to that, as near as might be, they returned: for it does not appear that any others, at least any that were able to oppose them, had possessed them in their absence. 4. That the leaders are first mentioned, <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.2">v. 2</reference>. Zerubbabel and Jeshua were their Moses and Aaron, the former their chief prince, the latter their chief priest. Nehemiah and Mordecai are mentioned here; some think not the same with the famous men we afterwards meet with of those names: probably they were the same, but afterwards returned to court for the service of their country. 5. Some of these several families are named from the persons that were their ancestors, others from the places in which they had formerly resided; as with us many surnames are the proper names of persons, others of places. 6. Some little difference there is between the numbers of some of the families here and in <reference osisRef="Neh.7.5-Neh.7.73">Neh. vii.</reference>, where this catalogue is repeated, which might arise from this, that some who had given in their names at first to come afterwards drew back—said, <hi type="italic">I go, Sir, but went not,</hi> which would lessen the number of the families they belonged to; others that declined, at first, <hi type="italic">afterwards repented and went,</hi> and so increased the number. 7. Here are two families that are called <hi type="italic">the children of Elam</hi> (one <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.7">v. 7</reference>, another <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.31">v. 31</reference>), and, which is strange, the number of both is the same, 1254. 8. The children of Adonikam, which signifies <hi type="italic">a high lord,</hi> were 666, just the <hi type="italic">number of the beast</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.13.18">Rev. xiii. 18</reference>), which is there said to be <hi type="italic">the number of a man,</hi> which, Mr. Hugh Broughton thinks, has reference to this man. 9. The children of Bethlehem (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.21">v. 21</reference>) were but 123, though it was David's city; for Bethlehem was <hi type="italic">little among the thousands of Judah,</hi> yet there must the Messiah arise, <reference osisRef="Mic.5.2">Mic. v. 2</reference>. 10. Anathoth had been a famous place in the tribe of Benjamin and yet here it numbered but 128 (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.23">v. 23</reference>), which is to be imputed to the divine curse which the men of Anathoth brought upon themselves by persecuting Jeremiah, who was of their city. <reference osisRef="Jer.11.21">Jer. xi. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.11.23">23</reference>, <hi type="italic">There shall be no remnant of them, for I will bring evil upon the men of Anathoth.</hi> And see <reference osisRef="Isa.10.30">Isa. x. 30</reference>, <hi type="italic">O poor Anathoth!</hi> Nothing brings ruin on a people sooner than persecution.

<div eID="gen8545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8546" type="x-p"/> Here is an account, I. Of the priests that returned, and they were a considerable number, about a tenth part of the whole company: for the whole were above 42,000 (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.64">v. 64</reference>), and four families of priests made up above 4200 (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.36-Ezra.2.39">v. 36-39</reference>); thus was the tenth God's part—a blessed decimation. Three of the fathers of the priests here named were heads of courses, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.7-1Chr.24.8">1 Chron. xxiv. 7, 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.14">14</reference>. The fourth was Pashur, <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.38">v. 38</reference>. If these were of the posterity of that Pashur that abused Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.20.1">Jer. xx. 1</reference>), it is strange that so bad a man should have so good a seed, and so numerous. <div eID="gen8546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8547" type="x-p"/> II. Of the Levites. I cannot but wonder at the small number of them, for, taking in both the singers and the porters (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.40-Ezra.2.42">v. 40-42</reference>), they did not make 350. Time was when the Levites were more forward to their duty than the priests (<reference osisRef="2Chr.29.34">2 Chron. xxix. 34</reference>), but they were not so now. If one place, one family, has the reputation for pious zeal now, another may have it another time. <hi type="italic">The wind blows where it listeth,</hi> and shifts its points. <div eID="gen8547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8548" type="x-p"/> III. Of the Nethinim, who, it is supposed, were the Gibeonites, <hi type="italic">given</hi> (so their name signifies) by Joshua first (<reference osisRef="Josh.9.27">Josh. ix. 27</reference>), and again by David (<reference osisRef="Ezra.8.20">Ezra viii. 20</reference>), when Saul had expelled them, to be employed by the Levites in the work of God's house as hewers of wood and drawers of water; and, with them, of the children of Solomon's servants, whom he gave for the like use (whether they were Jews or Gentiles does not appear) and who were here taken notice of among the retainers of the temple and numbered with the Nethinim, <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.55">v. 55</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.58">58</reference>. Note, It is an honour to belong to God's house, though in the meanest office there. <div eID="gen8548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8549" type="x-p"/> IV. Of some that were looked upon as Israelites by birth, and others as priests, and yet could not make out a clear title to the honour. 1. There were some that could not prove themselves Israelites (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.59-Ezra.2.60">v. 59, 60</reference>), a considerable number, who presumed they were of the seed of Jacob, but could not produce their pedigrees, and yet would go up to Jerusalem, having an affection to the house and people of God. These shamed those who were true-born Israelites, and yet were not called Israelites indeed, <hi type="italic">who came out of the waters of Judah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.48.1">Isa. xlviii. 1</reference>), but had lost the relish of those waters. 2. There were others that could not prove themselves priests, and yet were supposed to be of the seed of Aaron. What is not preserved in black and white will, in all likelihood, be forgotten in a little time. Now we are here told, (1.) How they lost their evidence. One of their ancestors married a daughter of Barzillai, that great man whom we read of in David's time; he gloried in an alliance to that honourable family, and, preferring that before the dignity of his priesthood, would have his children called after Barzillai's family, and their pedigree preserved in the registers of that house, not of the house of Aaron, and so they lost it. In Babylon there was nothing to be got by the priesthood, and therefore they cared not for being akin to it. Those who think their ministry, or their relation to ministers, a diminution or disparagement to them, forget who it was that said, <hi type="italic">I magnify my office.</hi> (2.) What they lost with it. It could not be taken for granted that they were priests when they could not produce their proofs, but they were, <hi type="italic">as polluted, put from the priesthood.</hi> Now that the priests had recovered their rights, and had the altar to live upon again, they would gladly be looked upon as priests. But they had sold their birthright for the honour of being gentlemen, and therefore were justly degraded, and forbidden to <hi type="italic">eat of the most holy things.</hi> Note, Christ will be ashamed of those that are ashamed of him and his service. It was the tirshatha, or governor, that put them under this sequestration, which some understand of Zerubbabel the present governor, others of Nehemiah (who is so called, <reference osisRef="Neh.8.9">Neh. viii. 9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Neh.10.1">x. 1</reference>, and who gave this order when he came some years after); but the prohibition was not absolute, it was only a suspension, till there should be a high priest <hi type="italic">with Urim and Thummin,</hi> by whom they might know God's mind in this matter. This, it seems, was expected and desired, but it does not appear that ever they were blessed with it under the second temple. They had the canon of the Old Testament complete, which was better than Urim; and, by the want of that oracle, they were taught to expect the Messiah the great Oracle, which the Urim and Thummim was but a type of. Nor does it appear that the second temple had the ark in it, either the old one or a new one. Those shadows by degrees vanished, as the substance approached; and God, by the prophet, intimates to his people that they should sustain no damage by the want of the ark, <reference osisRef="Jer.3.16-Jer.3.17">Jer. iii. 16, 17</reference>. <hi type="italic">In those days,</hi> when <hi type="italic">they shall call Jerusalem the throne of the Lord,</hi> and <hi type="italic">all the nations shall be gathered</hi> to it, they shall <hi type="italic">say no more, The ark of the covenant of the Lord, neither shall it come to mind,</hi> for they shall do very well without it.

<div eID="gen8549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8550" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">64</hi> The whole congregation together <hi type="italic">was</hi> forty and two thousand three hundred <hi type="italic">and</hi> threescore, <hi type="super">65</hi> Beside their servants and their maids, of whom <hi type="italic">there were</hi> seven thousand three hundred thirty and seven: and <hi type="italic">there were</hi> among them two hundred singing men and singing women. <hi type="super">66</hi> Their horses <hi type="italic">were</hi> seven hundred thirty and six; their mules, two hundred forty and five; <hi type="super">67</hi> Their camels, four hundred thirty and five; <hi type="italic">their</hi> asses, six thousand seven hundred and twenty. <hi type="super">68</hi> And <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the chief of the fathers, when they came to the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which <hi type="italic">is</hi> at Jerusalem, offered freely for the house of God to set it up in his place: <hi type="super">69</hi> They gave after their ability unto the treasure of the work threescore and one thousand drams of gold, and five thousand pound of silver, and one hundred priests' garments. <hi type="super">70</hi> So the priests, and the Levites, and <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the people, and the singers, and the porters, and the Nethinims, dwelt in their cities, and all Israel in their cities. <div eID="gen8550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8551" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The sum total of the company that returned out of Babylon. The particular sums before mentioned amount not quite to 30,000 (29,818), so that there were above 12,000 that come out into any of those accounts, who, it is probable, were of the rest of the tribes of Israel, besides Judah and Benjamin, that could not tell of what particular family or city they were, but that they were Israelites, and of what tribe. Now, 1. This was more than double the number that were carried captive into Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, so that, as in Egypt, the time of their affliction was the time of their increase. 2. These were but few to begin a nation with, and yet, by virtue of the old promise made to their fathers, they multiplied so as before their last destruction by the Romans, about 500 years after, to be a very numerous people. When God says, "Increase and multiply," <hi type="italic">a little one shall become a thousand.</hi> <div eID="gen8551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8552" type="x-p"/> II. Their retinue. They were themselves little better than servants, and therefore no wonder that their servants were comparatively but few (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.65">v. 65</reference>) and their beasts of burden about as many, <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.66-Ezra.2.67">v. 66, 67</reference>. It was not with them now as in days past. But notice is taken of 200 <hi type="italic">singing-men and women</hi> whom they had among them, who, we will suppose, were intended (as those <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.25">2 Chron. xxxv. 25</reference>) to excite <hi type="italic">their mourning,</hi> for it was foretold that they should, upon this occasion, <hi type="italic">go weeping</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.4">Jer. l. 4</reference>), with ditties of lamentation. <div eID="gen8552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8553" type="x-p"/> III. Their oblations. It is said (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.68-Ezra.2.69">v. 68, 69</reference>), 1. That they <hi type="italic">came to the house of the Lord at Jerusalem;</hi> and yet that house, that holy and beautiful house, was now in ruins, a heap of rubbish. But, like their father Abraham, when the altar was gone they came with devotion to <hi type="italic">the place of the altar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.13.4">Gen. xiii. 4</reference>); and it is the character of the genuine sons of Zion that they favour even <hi type="italic">the dust thereof,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.102.14">Ps. cii. 14</reference>. 2. That they offered freely towards the <hi type="italic">setting of it up in its place.</hi> That, it seems, was the first house they talked of setting up; and though they came off a journey, and were beginning the world (two chargeable things), yet they offered, and offered freely, towards the building of the temple. Let none complain of the necessary expenses of their religion, but believe that when they come to balance the account they will find that it clears the cost. Their offering was nothing in comparison with the offerings of the princes in David's time; then they offered by talents (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.7">1 Chron. xxix. 7</reference>), now by drams, yet these drams, being after their ability, were as acceptable to God as those talents, like the widow's two mites. The 61,000 drams of gold amount, by Cumberland's calculation, to so many pounds of our money and so many groats. Every maneh, or pound of silver, he reckons to be sixty shekels (that is, thirty ounces), which we may reckon 7<hi type="italic">l.</hi> 10<hi type="italic">s.</hi> of our money, so that this 5000 pounds of silver will be above 37,000<hi type="italic">l.</hi> of our money. It seems, God had blessed them with an increase of their wealth, as well as of their numbers, in Babylon; and, as God had prospered them, they gave cheerfully to the service of his house. 3. That they <hi type="italic">dwelt in their cities,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.70">v. 70</reference>. Though their cities were out of repair, yet, because they were their cities, such as God had assigned them, they were content to dwell in them, and were thankful for liberty and property, though they had little of pomp, plenty, or power. Their poverty was a bad cause, but their unity and unanimity were a good effect of it. Here was room enough for them all and all their substance, so that there was no strife among them, but perfect harmony, a blessed presage of their settlement, as their discords in the latter times of that state were of their ruin.  <chapter eID="Ezra.2"/> <div eID="gen8553" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen8556" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8555" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Renewal of the Sacrifices. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 536.)</title> <div sID="gen8557" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> And when the seventh month was come, and the children of Israel <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the cities, the people gathered themselves together as one man to Jerusalem. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then stood up Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and his brethren the priests, and Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and his brethren, and builded the altar of the God of Israel, to offer burnt offerings thereon, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> written in the law of Moses the man of God. <hi type="super">3</hi> And they set the altar upon his bases; for fear <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon them because of the people of those countries: and they offered burnt offerings thereon unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">even</hi> burnt offerings morning and evening. <hi type="super">4</hi> They kept also the feast of tabernacles, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> written, and <hi type="italic">offered</hi> the daily burnt offerings by number, according to the custom, as the duty of every day required; <hi type="super">5</hi> And afterward <hi type="italic">offered</hi> the continual burnt offering, both of the new moons, and of all the set feasts of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that were consecrated, and of every one that willingly offered a freewill offering unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">6</hi> From the first day of the seventh month began they to offer burnt offerings unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . But the foundation of the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was not <hi type="italic">yet</hi> laid. <hi type="super">7</hi> They gave money also unto the masons, and to the carpenters; and meat, and drink, and oil, unto them of Zidon, and to them of Tyre, to bring cedar trees from Lebanon to the sea of Joppa, according to the grant that they had of Cyrus king of Persia. <div eID="gen8557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8558" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. A general assembly of the returned Israelites at Jerusalem, in the <hi type="italic">seventh month,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.1">v. 1</reference>. We may suppose that they came from Babylon in the spring, and must allow at least four months for the journey, for so long Ezra and his company were in coming, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.9">ch. vii. 9</reference>. The seventh month therefore soon came, in which many of the feasts of the Lord were to be solemnized; and then they gathered themselves together by agreement among themselves, rather than by the command of authority, to Jerusalem. Though they had newly come to their cities, and had their hands full of business there, to provide necessaries for themselves and their families, which might have excused them from attending on God's altar till the hurry was a little over, as many foolishly put off their coming to the communion till they are settled in the world, yet such was their zeal for religion, now that they had newly come from under correction for their irreligion, that they left all their business in the country, to attend God's altar; and (which is strange) in this pious zeal they were all of a mind, they came <hi type="italic">as one man.</hi> Let worldly business be postponed to the business of religion and it will prosper the better. <div eID="gen8558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8559" type="x-p"/> II. The care which their leading men took to have an altar ready for them to attend upon. <div eID="gen8559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8560" type="x-p"/> 1. Joshua and his brethren the priests, Zerubbabel and his brethren the princes, built <hi type="italic">the altar of the God of Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.2">v. 2</reference>), in the same place (it is likely) where it had stood, upon the same bases, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.3">v. 3</reference>. Bishop Patrick, observing that before the temple was built there seems to have been a tabernacle pitched for the divine service, as was in David's time, not on Mount Moriah, but Mount Sion (<reference osisRef="1Chr.9.23">1 Chron. ix. 23</reference>), supposes that this altar was erected there, to be used while the temple was in building. Let us learn hence, (1.) To <hi type="italic">begin with God.</hi> The more difficult and necessitous our case is the more concerned we are to take him along with us in all our ways. If we expect to be directed by his oracles, let him be honoured by our offerings. (2.) To <hi type="italic">do what we can</hi> in the worship of God when <hi type="italic">we cannot do what we would.</hi> They could not immediately have a temple, but they would not be without an altar. Abraham, wherever he came, <hi type="italic">built an altar;</hi> and wherever we come, though we may perhaps want the benefit of the candlestick of preaching, and the showbread of the eucharist, yet, if we bring not the sacrifices of prayer and praise, we are wanting in our duty, for we have an altar that sanctifies the gift ever ready. <div eID="gen8560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8561" type="x-p"/> 2. Observe the reason here given why they hastened to set up the altar: <hi type="italic">Fear was upon them, because of the people of the land.</hi> They were in the midst of enemies that bore ill will to them and their religion, for whom they were an unequal match. And, (1.) <hi type="italic">Though</hi> they were so, yet they built the altar (so some read it); they would not be frightened from their religion by the opposition they were likely to meet with in it. Never let the fear of man bring us into this snare. (2.) <hi type="italic">Because</hi> they were so, therefore they set up the altar. Apprehension of danger should stir us up to our duty. Have we many enemies? Then it is good to have God our friend and to keep up our correspondence with him. This good use we should make of our fears, we should be driven by them to our knees. Even Saul would think himself undone if the enemy should come upon him before he had made his supplication to God, <reference osisRef="1Sam.13.12">1 Sam. xii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen8561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8562" type="x-p"/> III. The sacrifices they offered upon the altar. The altar was reared to be used, and they used it accordingly. Let not those that have an altar starve it. <div eID="gen8562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8563" type="x-p"/> 1. They began <hi type="italic">on the first day of the seventh month,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.6">v. 6</reference>. It does not appear that they had any fire from heaven to begin with, as Moses and Solomon had, but common fire served them, as it did the patriarchs. <div eID="gen8563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8564" type="x-p"/> 2. Having begun, they kept up the <hi type="italic">continual burnt-offering</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.5">v. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">morning and evening,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.3">v. 3</reference>. They had known by sad experience what it was to want the comfort of the daily sacrifice to plead in their daily prayers, and now that it was revived they resolved not to let it fall again. The daily lamb typified the Lamb of God, whose righteousness must be our confidence in all our prayers. <div eID="gen8564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8565" type="x-p"/> 3. They observed all the <hi type="italic">set feasts of the Lord,</hi> and offered the sacrifices appointed for each, and particularly <hi type="italic">the feast of tabernacles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.4-Ezra.3.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. Now that they had received such great mercy from God that joyful feast was in a special manner seasonable. And now that they were beginning to settle in their cities it might serve well to remind them of their fathers dwelling in tents in the wilderness. That feast also which had a peculiar reference to gospel times (as appears, <reference osisRef="Zech.14.18">Zech. xiv. 18</reference>) was brought, in a special manner, into reputation, now that those times drew on. Of the services of this feast, which continued seven days and had peculiar sacrifices appointed, it is said that they did <hi type="italic">as the duty of every day required</hi> (see <reference osisRef="Num.29.13-Num.29.38">Num. xxix. 13, 17</reference>, &c.), <hi type="italic">Verbum die in die suo—the word, or matter, of the day in its day</hi> (so it is in the original)—a phrase that has become proverbial with those that have used themselves to scripture-language. If the feast of tabernacles was a figure of a gospel conversation, in respect of continual weanedness from the world and joy in God, we may infer that it concerns us all to do the <hi type="italic">work of the day in its day, according as the duty of the day requires,</hi> that is, (1.) We must improve time, by finding some business to do every day that will turn to a good account. (2.) We must improve opportunity, by accommodating ourselves to that which is the proper business of the present day. Every thing is beautiful in its season. The tenth day of this month was the day of atonement, a solemn day, and very seasonable now: it is very probable that they observed it, yet it is not mentioned, nor indeed in all the Old Testament do I remember the least mention of the observance of that day; as if it were enough that we have the law of it in <reference osisRef="Lev.16.1-Lev.16.34">Lev. xvi.</reference>, and the gospel of it, which was the chief intention of it, in the New Testament. <div eID="gen8565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8566" type="x-p"/> 4. They offered <hi type="italic">every man's free-will offering,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.5">v. 5</reference>. The law required much, but they brought more; for, though they had little wealth to support the expense of their sacrifices, they had much zeal, and, we may suppose, spared at their own tables that they might plentifully supply God's altar. Happy are those that bring with them out of the furnace of affliction such a holy heat as this. <div eID="gen8566" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8567" type="x-p"/> IV. The preparation they made for the building of the temple, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.7">v. 7</reference>. This they applied themselves immediately to; for, while we do what we can, we must still be aiming to do more and better. Tyre and Sidon must now, as of old, furnish them with workmen, and Lebanon with timber, orders for both which they had from Cyrus. What God calls us to we may depend upon his providence to furnish us for.

<div eID="gen8567" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Foundation of the Temple Laid. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 535.)</title> <div sID="gen8568" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Now in the second year of their coming unto the house of God at Jerusalem, in the second month, began Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and the remnant of their brethren the priests and the Levites, and all they that were come out of the captivity unto Jerusalem; and appointed the Levites, from twenty years old and upward, to set forward the work of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> Then stood Jeshua <hi type="italic">with</hi> his sons and his brethren, Kadmiel and his sons, the sons of Judah, together, to set forward the workmen in the house of God: the sons of Henadad, <hi type="italic">with</hi> their sons and their brethren the Levites. <hi type="super">10</hi> And when the builders laid the foundation of the temple of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , they set the priests in their apparel with trumpets, and the Levites the sons of Asaph with cymbals, to praise the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , after the ordinance of David king of Israel. <hi type="super">11</hi> And they sang together by course in praising and giving thanks unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; because <hi type="italic">he is</hi> good, for his mercy <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever toward Israel. And all the people shouted with a great shout, when they praised the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , because the foundation of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was laid. <hi type="super">12</hi> But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, <hi type="italic">who were</hi> ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy: <hi type="super">13</hi> So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people: for the people shouted with a loud shout, and the noise was heard afar off. <div eID="gen8568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8569" type="x-p"/> There was no dispute among the returned Jews whether they should build the temple or no; that was immediately resolved on, and that it should be done with all speed; what comfort could they take in their own land if they had not that token of God's presence with them and the record of his name among them? We have here therefore an account of the beginning of that good work. Observe, <div eID="gen8569" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8570" type="x-p"/> I. When it was begun-in the second month of the second year, as soon as ever the season of the year would permit (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.8">v. 8</reference>), and when they had ended the solemnities of the passover. They took little more than half a year for making preparation of the ground and materials; so much were their hearts upon it. Note, When any good work is to be done it will be our wisdom to set about it quickly, and not to lose time, yea, though we foresee difficulty and opposition in it. Thus we engage ourselves to it, and engage God for us. Well begun (we say) is half ended. <div eID="gen8570" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8571" type="x-p"/> II. Who began it—Zerubbabel, and Jeshua, and their brethren. Then the work of God is likely to go on well when magistrates, ministers, and people, are hearty for it, and agree in their places to promote it. It was God that gave them one heart for this service, and it boded well. <div eID="gen8571" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8572" type="x-p"/> III. Who were employed to further it. They appointed the <hi type="italic">Levites to set forward the work</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.8">v. 8</reference>), and they did it by <hi type="italic">setting forward the workmen</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.9">v. 9</reference>), and strengthening their hands with good and comfortable words. Note, Those that do not work themselves may yet do good service by quickening and encouraging those that do work. <div eID="gen8572" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8573" type="x-p"/> IV. How God was praised at the laying of the foundation of the temple (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.10-Ezra.3.11">v. 10, 11</reference>); the priests with the trumpets appointed by Moses, and the Levites with the cymbals appointed by David, made up a concert of music, not to please the ear, but to assist the singing of that everlasting hymn which will never be out of date, and to which our tongues should never be out of tune, <hi type="italic">God is good, and his mercy endureth for ever,</hi> the burden of <reference osisRef="Ps.136.1-Ps.136.26">Ps. cxxxvi.</reference> Let all the streams of mercy be traced up to the fountain. Whatever our condition is, how many soever our griefs and fears, let it be owned that God is good; and, whatever fails, that his mercy fails not. Let this be sung with application, as here; not only his mercy endures for ever, but it endures for ever towards Israel, Israel when captives in a strange land and strangers in their own land. However it be, yet <hi type="italic">God is good to Israel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.1">Ps. lxxiii. 1</reference>), good to us. Let the reviving of the church's interests, when they seemed dead, be ascribed to the continuance of God's mercy for ever, for therefore the church continues. <div eID="gen8573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8574" type="x-p"/> V. How the people were affected. A remarkable mixture of various affections there was upon this occasion. Different sentiments there were among the people of God, and each expressed himself according to his sentiments, and yet there was no disagreement among them, their minds were not alienated from each other nor the common concern retarded by it. 1. Those that only knew the misery of having no temple at all praised the Lord with shouts of joy when they saw but the foundation of one laid, <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.11">v. 11</reference>. To them even this foundation seemed great, and was as life from the dead; to their hungry souls even this was sweet. They shouted, so that <hi type="italic">the noise was heard afar off.</hi> Note, We ought to be thankful for the beginnings of mercy, though we have not yet come to the perfection of it; and the foundations of a temple, after long desolations, cannot but be fountains of joy to every faithful Israelite. 2. Those that remembered the glory of the first temple which Solomon built, and considered how far this was likely to be inferior to that, perhaps in dimensions, certainly in magnificence and sumptuousness, <hi type="italic">wept with a loud voice,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.3.12">v. 12</reference>. If we date the captivity with the first, from the fourth of Jehoiakim, it was about fifty-two years since the temple was burnt; if from Jeconiah's captivity, it was but fifty-nine. So that many now alive might remember it standing; and a great mercy it was to the captives that they had the lives of so many of their priests and Levites lengthened out, who could tell them what they themselves remembered of the glory of Jerusalem, to quicken them in their return. These lamented the disproportion between this temple and the former. And, (1.) There was some reason for it; and if they turned their tears into the right channel, and bewailed the sin that was the cause of this melancholy change, they did well. Sin sullies the glory of any church or people, and, when they find themselves diminished and brought low, that must bear the blame. (2.) Yet it was their infirmity to mingle those tears with the common joys and so to cast a damp upon them. They <hi type="italic">despised the day of small things,</hi> and were unthankful for the good they enjoyed, because it was not so much as their ancestors had, though it was much more than they deserved. In the harmony of public joys, let not us be jarring strings. It was an aggravation of the discouragement they hereby gave to the people that they were priests and Levites, who should have known and taught others how to be duly affected under various providences, and not to let the remembrance of former afflictions drown the sense of present mercies. This mixture of sorrow and joy here is a representation of this world. Some are bathing in rivers of joy, while others are drowned in floods of tears. In heaven all are singing, and none sighing; in hell all are weeping and wailing, and none rejoicing; but here on earth we can scarcely <hi type="italic">discern the shouts of joy from the noise of the weeping.</hi> Let us learn to <hi type="italic">rejoice with those that do rejoice</hi> and <hi type="italic">weep with those that weep,</hi> and ourselves to rejoice as though we rejoiced not, and weep as though we wept not.  <chapter eID="Ezra.3"/> <div eID="gen8574" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen8577" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8576" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Opposition Made to the Jews. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 535.)</title> <div sID="gen8578" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the children of the captivity builded the temple unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel; <hi type="super">2</hi> Then they came to Zerubbabel, and to the chief of the fathers, and said unto them, Let us build with you: for we seek your God, as ye <hi type="italic">do;</hi> and we do sacrifice unto him since the days of Esarhaddon king of Assur, which brought us up hither. <hi type="super">3</hi> But Zerubbabel, and Jeshua, and the rest of the chief of the fathers of Israel, said unto them, Ye have nothing to do with us to build a house unto our God; but we ourselves together will build unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, as king Cyrus the king of Persia hath commanded us. <hi type="super">4</hi> Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building, <hi type="super">5</hi> And hired counsellors against them, to frustrate their purpose, all the days of Cyrus king of Persia, even until the reign of Darius king of Persia. <div eID="gen8578" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8579" type="x-p"/> We have here an instance of the old enmity that was put between the seed of the woman and the seed of the serpent. God's temple cannot be built, but Satan will rage, and the <hi type="italic">gates of hell</hi> will <hi type="italic">fight against it.</hi> The gospel kingdom was, in like manner, to be set up with much struggling and contention. In this respect the glory of the latter house was greater than the glory of the former, and it was more a figure of the temple of Christ's church, in that Solomon built his temple when there was <hi type="italic">no adversary nor evil occurrent,</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.4">1 Kings v. 4</reference>); but this second temple was built notwithstanding great opposition, in the removing and conquering of which, and the bringing of the work to perfection at last in spite of it, the wisdom, power, and goodness of God were much glorified, and the church was encouraged to trust in him. <div eID="gen8579" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8580" type="x-p"/> I. The undertakers are here called the <hi type="italic">children of the captivity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.1">v. 1</reference>), which makes them look very little. They had newly come out of captivity, were born in captivity, had still the marks of their captivity upon them; though they were not now captives, they were under the control of those whose captives they had lately been. Israel was God's son, his first-born; but by their iniquity the people sold and enslaved themselves, and so became children of the captivity. But, it should seem, the thought of their being so quickened them to this work, for it was by their neglect of the temple that they lost their freedom. <div eID="gen8580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8581" type="x-p"/> II. The opposers of the undertaking are here said to be <hi type="italic">the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin,</hi> not the Chaldeans or Persians (they gave them no disturbance—"let them build and welcome"), but the relics of the ten tribes, and the foreigners that had joined themselves to them, and patched up that mongrel religion we had an account of, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.33">2 Kings xvii. 33</reference>. <hi type="italic">They feared the Lord, and served their own gods too.</hi> They are called <hi type="italic">the people of the land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.4">v. 4</reference>. The worst enemies Judah and Benjamin had were those that <hi type="italic">said they were Jews and were not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.9">Rev. iii. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen8581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8582" type="x-p"/> III. The opposition they gave had in it much of the subtlety of the old serpent. When they heard that the temple was in building they were immediately aware that it would be a fatal blow to their superstition, and set themselves to oppose it. They had not power to do it forcibly, but they tried all the ways they could to do it effectually. <div eID="gen8582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8583" type="x-p"/> 1. They offered their service to build with the Israelites only that thereby they might get an opportunity to retard the work, while they pretended to further it. Now, (1.) Their offer was plausible enough, and looked kind: "<hi type="italic">We will build with you,</hi> will help you to contrive, and will contribute towards the expense; <hi type="italic">for we seek your God as you do,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.2">v. 2</reference>. This was false, for, though they sought the same God, they did not seek him only, nor seek him in the way he appointed, and therefore did not seek him as they did. Herein they designed, if it were possible, to hinder the building of it, at least to hinder their comfortable enjoyment of it; as good almost not have it as not have it to themselves, for the pure worship of the true God and him only. Thus are the <hi type="italic">kisses of an enemy deceitful;</hi> his words are smoother than butter when war is in his heart. But, (2.) The refusal of their proffered service was very just, <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.3">v. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">The chief of the fathers of Israel</hi> were soon aware that they meant them no kindness, whatever they pretended, but really designed to do them a mischief, and therefore (though they had need enough of help if it had been such as they could confide in) told them plainly, "<hi type="italic">You have nothing to do with us,</hi> have no part nor lot in this matter, are not true-born Israelites nor faithful worshippers of God; <hi type="italic">you worship you know not what,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.22">John iv. 22</reference>. You are none of those with whom we dare hold communion, and therefore we ourselves will build it." They plead not to them the law of their God, which forbade them to mingle with strangers (though that especially they had an eye to), but that which they would take more notice of, the king's commission, which was directed to them only: "The king of Persia has commanded us to build this house, and we shall distrust and affront him if we call in foreign aid." Note, In doing good there is need of the <hi type="italic">wisdom of the serpent,</hi> as well as the <hi type="italic">innocency of the dove,</hi> and we have need, as it follows there, to <hi type="italic">beware of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.16-Matt.10.17">Matt. x. 16, 17</reference>. We should carefully consider with whom we are associated and on whose hand we lean. While we trust God with a pious confidence we must trust men with a prudent jealousy and caution. <div eID="gen8583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8584" type="x-p"/> 2. When this plot failed they did what they could to divert them from the work and discourage them in it. They weakened their hands by telling them it was in vain to attempt it, calling them <hi type="italic">foolish builders,</hi> who began what they were not able to finish, and by their insinuations troubled them, and made them drive heavily in the work. All were not alike zealous in it. Those that were cool and indifferent were by these artifices drawn off from the work, which wanted their help, <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.4">v. 4</reference>. And because what they themselves said the Jews would suspect to be ill meant, and not be influenced by, they, underhand, <hi type="italic">hired counsellors against them,</hi> who, pretending to advise them for the best, should dissuade them from proceeding, and so <hi type="italic">frustrate their purpose</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.5">v. 5</reference>), or dissuade the men of Tyre and Sidon from furnishing them with the timber they had bargained for (<reference osisRef="Ezra.3.7">ch. iii. 7</reference>); or whatever business they had at the Persian court, to solicit for any particular grants or favours, pursuant to the general edict for their liberty, there were those that were hired and lay ready to appear of counsel against them. Wonder not at the restlessness of the church's enemies in their attempts against the building of God's temple. He whom they serve, and whose work they are doing, is <hi type="italic">unwearied</hi> in <hi type="italic">walking to and fro through the earth</hi> to do mischief. And let those who discourage a good work, and weaken the hands of those that are employed in it, see whose pattern they follow.

<div eID="gen8584" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Jews Misrepresented. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 521.)</title> <div sID="gen8585" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And in the reign of Ahasuerus, in the beginning of his reign, wrote they <hi type="italic">unto him</hi> an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem. <hi type="super">7</hi> And in the days of Artaxerxes wrote Bishlam, Mithredath, Tabeel, and the rest of their companions, unto Artaxerxes king of Persia; and the writing of the letter <hi type="italic">was</hi> written in the Syrian tongue, and interpreted in the Syrian tongue. <hi type="super">8</hi> Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king in this sort: <hi type="super">9</hi> Then <hi type="italic">wrote</hi> Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions; the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the Elamites, <hi type="super">10</hi> And the rest of the nations whom the great and noble Asnappar brought over, and set in the cities of Samaria, and the rest <hi type="italic">that are</hi> on this side the river, and at such a time. <hi type="super">11</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the copy of the letter that they sent unto him, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto Artaxerxes the king; Thy servants the men on this side the river, and at such a time. <hi type="super">12</hi> Be it known unto the king, that the Jews which came up from thee to us are come unto Jerusalem, building the rebellious and the bad city, and have set up the walls <hi type="italic">thereof,</hi> and joined the foundations. <hi type="super">13</hi> Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up <hi type="italic">again, then</hi> will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and <hi type="italic">so</hi> thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings. <hi type="super">14</hi> Now because we have maintenance from <hi type="italic">the king's</hi> palace, and it was not meet for us to see the king's dishonour, therefore have we sent and certified the king; <hi type="super">15</hi> That search may be made in the book of the records of thy fathers: so shalt thou find in the book of the records, and know that this city <hi type="italic">is</hi> a rebellious city, and hurtful unto kings and provinces, and that they have moved sedition within the same of old time: for which cause was this city destroyed. <hi type="super">16</hi> We certify the king that, if this city be builded <hi type="italic">again,</hi> and the walls thereof set up, by this means thou shalt have no portion on this side the river. <div eID="gen8585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8586" type="x-p"/> Cyrus stedfastly adhered to the Jews' interest, and supported his own grant. It was to no purpose to offer any thing to him in prejudice of it. What he did was from a good principle, and in the fear of God, and therefore he adhered to it. But, though his reign in all was thirty years, yet after the conquest of Babylon, and his decree for the release of the Jews, some think that he reigned but three years, others seven, and then either died or gave up that part of his government, in which his successor was Ahasuerus (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.6">v. 6</reference>), called also <hi type="italic">Artaxerxes</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.7">v. 7</reference>), supposed to be the same that in heathen authors is called <hi type="italic">Cambyses,</hi> who had never taken such cognizance of the despised Jews as to concern himself for them, nor had he that knowledge of the God of Israel which his predecessor had. To him these Samaritans applied by letter for an order to stop the building of the temple; and they did it in the beginning of his reign, being resolved to lose no time when they thought they had a king for their purpose. See how watchful the church's enemies are to take the first opportunity of doing it a mischief; let not its friends be less careful to do it a kindness. Here is, <div eID="gen8586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8587" type="x-p"/> I. The general purport of the letter which they sent to the king, to inform him of this matter. It is called (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.6">v. 6</reference>) <hi type="italic">an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem.</hi> The devil is the <hi type="italic">accuser of the brethren</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.10">Rev. xii. 10</reference>), and he carries on his malicious designs against them, not only by accusing them himself before God, as he did Job, but by acting as a lying spirit in the mouths of his instruments, whom he employs to accuse them before magistrates and kings and to make them odious to the many and obnoxious to the mighty. Marvel not if the same arts be still used to depreciate serious godliness. <div eID="gen8587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8588" type="x-p"/> II. The persons concerned in writing this letter. The contrivers are named (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.7">v. 7</reference>) that plotted the thing, the writers (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.8">v. 8</reference>) that put it into form, and the subscribers (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.9">v. 9</reference>) that concurred in it and joined with them in this representation, this misrepresentation I should call it. Now see here, 1. How the <hi type="italic">rulers take counsel together against the Lord</hi> and his temple, with their companions. The building of the temple would do them no harm, yet they appear against it with the utmost concern and virulence, perhaps because the prophets of the God of Israel had foretold the <hi type="italic">famishing</hi> and <hi type="italic">perishing</hi> of all the <hi type="italic">gods of the heathen,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.11">Zeph. ii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.11">Jer. x. 11</reference>. 2. How the people concurred with them in imagining this vain thing. They followed the cry, though ignorant of the merits of the cause. All the several colonies of that plantation (nine are here mentioned), who had their denomination from the cities or countries of Assyria, Chaldea, Persia, &c., whence they came, set their hands, by their representatives, to this letter. Perhaps they were incensed against these returned Jews because many of the ten tribes were among them, whose estates they had got into their possession, and of whom they were therefore jealous, lest they should attempt the recovery of them hereafter. <div eID="gen8588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8589" type="x-p"/> III. A copy of the letter itself, which Ezra inserts here out of the records of the kingdom of Persia, into which it had been entered; and it is well we have it, that we may see whence the like methods, still taken to expose good people and baffle good designs, are copied. <div eID="gen8589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8590" type="x-p"/> 1. They represent themselves as very loyal to the government, and greatly concerned for the honour and interest of it, and would have it thought that the king had no such loving faithful subjects in all his dominions as they were, none so sensible of their obligations to him, <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.14">v. 14</reference>. <hi type="italic">Because we are salted with the salt of the palace</hi> (so it is in the <hi type="italic">margin</hi>), "we have our salary from the court, and could no more live without it than flesh could be preserved without salt;" or, as some think, their pay or pension was sent them in salt; or "Because we had our education in the palace, and were brought up at the king's table," as we find, <reference osisRef="Dan.1.5">Dan. i. 5</reference>. These were those whom he intended to prefer; they did <hi type="italic">eat their portion of the king's meat.</hi> "Now, in consideration of this, <hi type="italic">it is not meet for us to see the king's dishonour;</hi>" and therefore they urge him to stop the building of the temple, which would certainly be the king's dishonour more than any thing else. Note, A secret enmity to Christ and his gospel is often gilded over with a pretended affection to Caesar and his power. The Jews hated the Roman government, and yet, to serve a turn, could cry, <hi type="italic">We have no king but Caesar.</hi> But (to allude to this), if those that lived upon the crown thought themselves bound in gratitude thus to support the interest of it, much more reason have we thus to argue ourselves into a pious concern for God's honour; <hi type="italic">we have our maintenance from the God of heaven</hi> and are <hi type="italic">salted with his salt,</hi> live upon his bounty and are the care of his providence; and therefore it is not <hi type="italic">meet for us to see his dishonour</hi> without resenting it and doing what we can to prevent it. <div eID="gen8590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8591" type="x-p"/> 2. They represent the Jews as disloyal, and dangerous to the government, that Jerusalem was <hi type="italic">the rebellious and bad city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">hurtful to kings and provinces,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.15">v. 15</reference>. See how Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">the joy of the whole earth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.48.2">Ps. xlviii. 2</reference>), is here reproached as the scandal of the whole earth. The enemies of the church could not do the bad things they design against it if they did not first give it a bad name. Jerusalem had been a loyal city to its rightful princes, and its present inhabitants were as well affected to the king and his government as any of his provinces whatsoever. Daniel, who was a Jew, had lately approved himself so faithful to his prince that his worst enemies could find no fault in his management, <reference osisRef="Dan.6.4">Dan. vi. 4</reference>. But thus was Elijah most unjustly charged with troubling Israel, the apostles with <hi type="italic">turning the world upside down,</hi> and Christ himself with <hi type="italic">perverting the nation</hi> and <hi type="italic">forbidding to give tribute to Caesar;</hi> and we must not think it strange if the same game be still played. Now here, <div eID="gen8591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8592" type="x-p"/> (1.) Their history of what was past was invidious, that <hi type="italic">within this city sedition had been moved of old time,</hi> and, for <hi type="italic">that cause, it was destroyed,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.15">v. 15</reference>.
