It cannot be denied but that there was some colour given for this suggestion by the attempts of Jehoiakim and Zedekiah to shake off the yoke of the king of Babylon, which, if they had kept close to their religion and the temple they were now rebuilding, they would never have come under. But it must be considered, [1.] That they were themselves, and their ancestors, sovereign princes, and their efforts to recover their rights, if there had not been in them the violation of an oath, for aught I know, would have been justifiable, and successful too, had they taken the right method and made their peace with God first. [2.] Though these Jews, and their princes, had been guilty of rebellion, yet it was unjust therefore to fasten this as an indelible brand upon this city, as if that must for ever after go under the name of <hi type="italic">the rebellious and bad city.</hi> The Jews, in their captivity, had given such specimens of good behaviour as were sufficient, with any reasonable men, to roll away that one reproach; for they were instructed (and we have reason to hope that they observed their instructions) to <hi type="italic">seek the peace of the city where</hi> they were <hi type="italic">captives</hi> and <hi type="italic">pray to the Lord for it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.29.7">Jer. xxix. 7</reference>. It was therefore very unfair, though not uncommon, thus to impute the iniquity of the fathers to the children. <div eID="gen8592" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8593" type="x-p"/> (2.) Their information concerning what was now doing was grossly false in matter of fact. Very careful they were to inform the king that the Jews had <hi type="italic">set up the walls of this city,</hi> nay, had <hi type="italic">finished</hi> them (so it is in the <hi type="italic">margin</hi>) and <hi type="italic">joined the foundations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.12">v. 12</reference>), when this was far from being the case. They had only begun to build the temple, which Cyrus commanded them to do, but, as for the walls, there was nothing done nor designed towards the repair of them, as appears by the condition they were in many years after (<reference osisRef="Neh.1.3">Neh. i. 3</reference>), all in ruins. <hi type="italic">What shall be given,</hi> and what <hi type="italic">done, to these false tongues,</hi> nay, which is worse, these false pens? <hi type="italic">sharp arrows,</hi> doubtless, <hi type="italic">of the mighty,</hi> and <hi type="italic">coals of juniper,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.120.3-Ps.120.4">Ps. cxx. 3, 4</reference>. If they had not been perfectly lost to all virtue and honour they would not, and if they had not been very secure of the king's countenance they durst not, have written that to the king which all their neighbours knew to be a notorious lie. See <reference osisRef="Prov.29.12">Prov. xxix. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen8593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8594" type="x-p"/> (3.) Their prognostics of the consequences were altogether groundless and absurd. They were very confident, and would have the king believe it upon their word, that if this city should be built, not only the Jews would <hi type="italic">pay no toll, tribute, or custom</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.13">v. 13</reference>), but (since a great lie is as soon spoken as a little one) that the king would have no portion at all on this side the river (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.16">v. 16</reference>), that all the countries on this side Euphrates would instantly revolt, drawn in to do so by their example; and, if the prince in possession should connive at this, he would wrong, not only himself, but his successors: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings.</hi> See how every line in this letter breathes both the subtlety and malice of the old serpent.

<div eID="gen8594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8595" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">Then</hi> sent the king an answer unto Rehum the chancellor, and <hi type="italic">to</hi> Shimshai the scribe, and <hi type="italic">to</hi> the rest of their companions that dwell in Samaria, and <hi type="italic">unto</hi> the rest beyond the river, Peace, and at such a time. <hi type="super">18</hi> The letter which ye sent unto us hath been plainly read before me. <hi type="super">19</hi> And I commanded, and search hath been made, and it is found that this city of old time hath made insurrection against kings, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> rebellion and sedition have been made therein. <hi type="super">20</hi> There have been mighty kings also over Jerusalem, which have ruled over all <hi type="italic">countries</hi> beyond the river; and toll, tribute, and custom, was paid unto them. <hi type="super">21</hi> Give ye now commandment to cause these men to cease, and that this city be not builded, until <hi type="italic">another</hi> commandment shall be given from me. <hi type="super">22</hi> Take heed now that ye fail not to do this: why should damage grow to the hurt of the kings? <hi type="super">23</hi> Now when the copy of king Artaxerxes' letter <hi type="italic">was</hi> read before Rehum, and Shimshai the scribe, and their companions, they went up in haste to Jerusalem unto the Jews, and made them to cease by force and power. <hi type="super">24</hi> Then ceased the work of the house of God which <hi type="italic">is</hi> at Jerusalem. So it ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia. <div eID="gen8595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8596" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen8596" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8597" type="x-p"/> I. The orders which the king of Persia gave, in answer to the information sent him by the Samaritans against the Jews. He suffered himself to be imposed upon by their fraud and falsehood, took no care to examine the allegations of their petition concerning that which the Jews were now doing, but took it for granted that the charge was true, and was very willing to gratify them with an order of council to stay proceedings. 1. He consulted the records concerning Jerusalem, and found that it had indeed rebelled against the king of Babylon, and therefore that it was, as they called it, a <hi type="italic">bad city</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.19">v. 19</reference>), and withal that in times past kings had reigned there, to whom all the countries on that side the river had been tributaries (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.20">v. 20</reference>), and that therefore there was danger that if ever they were able (which they were never likely to be) they would claim them again. Thus he says as they said, and pretends to give a reason for so doing. See the hard fate of princes, who must see and hear with other men's eyes and ears, and give judgment upon things as they are represented to them, though often represented falsely. God's judgment is always just because he sees things as they are, and it is according to truth. 2. He appointed these Samaritans to stop the building of the city immediately, till further orders should be given about it, <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.21-Ezra.4.22">v. 21, 22</reference>. Neither they, in their letter, nor he, in his order, make any mention of the temple, and the building of that, because both they and he knew that they had not only a permission, but a command, from Cyrus to rebuild that, which even these Samaritans had not the confidence to move for the repeal of. They spoke only of the <hi type="italic">city:</hi> "Let not <hi type="italic">that</hi> be built," that is, as a city with walls and gates; "whatever you do, prevent <hi type="italic">that, lest damage grow to the hurt of the kings:</hi>" he would not that the crown should lose by his wearing it. <div eID="gen8597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8598" type="x-p"/> II. The use which the enemies of the Jews made of these orders, so fraudulently obtained; upon the receipt of them they went up <hi type="italic">in haste to Jerusalem,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.23">v. 23</reference>. <hi type="italic">Their feet ran to evil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.1.16">Prov. i. 16</reference>. They were impatient till the builders were served with this prohibition, which they produced as their warrant to <hi type="italic">make them cease by force and power.</hi> As they abused the king in obtaining this order by their mis-informations, so they abused him in the execution of it; for the order was only to prevent the walling of the <hi type="italic">city,</hi> but, having force and power on their side, they construed it as relating to the <hi type="italic">temple,</hi> for it was that to which they had an ill will, and which they only wanted some colour to hinder the building of. There was indeed a general clause in the order, to <hi type="italic">cause these men to cease,</hi> which had reference to their complaint about building the walls; but they applied it to the building of the temple. See what need we have to pray, not only for kings, but for all in authority under them, and <hi type="italic">the governors sent by them,</hi> because the <hi type="italic">quietness</hi> and <hi type="italic">peaceableness</hi> of our lives, <hi type="italic">in all godliness and honesty,</hi> depend very much upon the integrity and wisdom of inferior magistrates, as well as the supreme. The consequence was that <hi type="italic">the work of the house of God ceased</hi> for a time, through the power and insolence of its enemies; and so, through the coldness and indifference of its friends, it stood still till the second year of Darius Hystaspes, for to me it seems clear by the thread of this sacred history that it was that Darius, <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.24">v. 24</reference>. Though now a stop was put to it by the violence of the Samaritans, yet that they might soon after have gone on by connivance, if they had had a due affection to the work, appears by this, that before they had that express warrant from the king for doing it (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.1-Ezra.6.12">ch. vi.</reference>) they were reproved by the prophets for not doing it, <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.1">ch. v. 1</reference>, compared with <reference osisRef="Hag.1.1">Hag. i. 1</reference>, &c. If they had taken due care to inform Cambyses of the truth of this case, perhaps he would have recalled his order; but, for aught I know, some of the builders were almost as willing it should cease as the adversaries themselves were. At some periods the church has suffered more by the coldness of its friends than by the heat of its enemies; but both together commonly make church-work slow work.  <chapter eID="Ezra.4"/> <div eID="gen8598" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen8601" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8600" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Jews Encouraged by Their Prophets. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 520.)</title> <div sID="gen8602" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then the prophets, Haggai the prophet, and Zechariah the son of Iddo, prophesied unto the Jews that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in Judah and Jerusalem in the name of the God of Israel, <hi type="italic">even</hi> unto them. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then rose up Zerubbabel the son of Shealtiel, and Jeshua the son of Jozadak, and began to build the house of God which <hi type="italic">is</hi> at Jerusalem: and with them <hi type="italic">were</hi> the prophets of God helping them. <div eID="gen8602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8603" type="x-p"/> Some reckon that the building of the temple was suspended for only nine years; I am willing to believe that fifteen years were the utmost. During this time they had an altar and a tabernacle, which no doubt they made use of. When we cannot do what we would we must do what we can in the service of God, and be sorry we can do no better. But the counsellors that were hired to hinder the work (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.5">ch. iv. 5</reference>) told them, and perhaps with a pretence to inspiration, that the time had not come for the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.2">Hag. i. 2</reference>), urging that it was long ere the time came for the building of Solomon's temple; and thus the people were made easy in their own <hi type="italic">ceiled houses,</hi> while <hi type="italic">God's house lay waste.</hi> Now here we are told how life was put into that good cause which seemed to lie dead. <div eID="gen8603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8604" type="x-p"/> I. They had two good ministers, who, in God's name, earnestly persuaded them to put the wheel of business in motion again. Observe, <div eID="gen8604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8605" type="x-p"/> 1. Who these ministers were, namely, the prophets Haggai and Zechariah, who both began to prophesy in the second year of Darius, as appears, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.1">Hag. i. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.1.1">Zech. i. 1</reference>. Note, (1.) The temple of God among men is to be built by prophecy, not by secular force (that often hinders it, but seldom furthers it), but by <hi type="italic">the word of God.</hi> As the <hi type="italic">weapons of our warfare,</hi> so the instruments of our building, <hi type="italic">are not carnal,</hi> but <hi type="italic">spiritual,</hi> and they are the ministers of the gospel that are the master-builders. (2.) It is the business of God's prophets to stir up God's people to that which is good, and to help them in it, to strengthen their hands, and, by suitable considerations fetched from the word of God, to quicken them to their duty and encourage them in it. (3.) It is a sign that God has mercy in store for a people when he raises up prophets among them to be their helpers in the way and work of God, their guides, overseers, and rulers. <div eID="gen8605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8606" type="x-p"/> 2. To whom they were sent. They prophesied unto the <hi type="italic">Jews</hi> (for, as to them pertained the giving of the law, so also the gift of prophecy, and therefore they are called <hi type="italic">the children of the prophets,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.3.25">Acts iii. 25</reference>, because they were educated under their tuition and instruction), <hi type="italic">even unto them, upon them,</hi> even <hi type="italic">upon them</hi> (so it is in the original), as Ezekiel prophesied <hi type="italic">upon the dry bones,</hi> that they might live, <reference osisRef="Ezek.37.4">Ezek. xxxvii. 4</reference>. They prophesied <hi type="italic">against</hi> them (so bishop Patrick), for they reproved them because they did not build the temple. The word of God, if it be not received now as a testimony to us, will be received another day as a testimony against us, and will judge us. <div eID="gen8606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8607" type="x-p"/> 3. Who sent them. They prophesied in the name, or (as some read it) <hi type="italic">in the cause,</hi> or for the sake, <hi type="italic">of the God of Israel;</hi> they spoke by commission from him, and argued from his authority over them, his interest in them, and the concern of his glory among them. <div eID="gen8607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8608" type="x-p"/> II. They had two good magistrates, who were forward and active in this work. Zerubbabel their chief prince, and Jeshua their chief priest, <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.2">v. 2</reference>. Those that are in places of dignity and power ought with their dignity to put honour upon and with their power to put life into every good work: thus it becomes those that preceded, and those that preside, with an exemplary care and zeal to <hi type="italic">fulfil all righteousness</hi> and to <hi type="italic">go before in a good work.</hi> These great men thought it no disparagement to them, but a happiness, to be taught and prescribed to by the prophets of the Lord, and were glad of their help in reviving this good work. Read the <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.1-Ezra.5.2 Hag.1.1-Hag.1.15">first chapter of the prophecy of Haggai</reference> here (for that is the best comment on these two verses) and see what great things God does by his word, which he magnifies above all his name, and by his Spirit working with it.

<div eID="gen8608" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Case Represented to Darius. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 519.)</title> <div sID="gen8609" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> At the same time came to them Tatnai, governor on this side the river, and Shethar-boznai, and their companions, and said thus unto them, Who hath commanded you to build this house, and to make up this wall? <hi type="super">4</hi> Then said we unto them after this manner, What are the names of the men that make this building? <hi type="super">5</hi> But the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews, that they could not cause them to cease, till the matter came to Darius: and then they returned answer by letter concerning this <hi type="italic">matter.</hi> <hi type="super">6</hi> The copy of the letter that Tatnai, governor on this side the river, and Shethar-boznai, and his companions the Apharsachites, which <hi type="italic">were</hi> on this side the river, sent unto Darius the king: <hi type="super">7</hi> They sent a letter unto him, wherein was written thus; Unto Darius the king, all peace. <hi type="super">8</hi> Be it known unto the king, that we went into the province of Judea, to the house of the great God, which is builded with great stones, and timber is laid in the walls, and this work goeth fast on, and prospereth in their hands. <hi type="super">9</hi> Then asked we those elders, <hi type="italic">and</hi> said unto them thus, Who commanded you to build this house, and to make up these walls? <hi type="super">10</hi> We asked their names also, to certify thee, that we might write the names of the men that <hi type="italic">were</hi> the chief of them. <hi type="super">11</hi> And thus they returned us answer, saying, We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth, and build the house that was builded these many years ago, which a great king of Israel builded and set up. <hi type="super">12</hi> But after that our fathers had provoked the God of heaven unto wrath, he gave them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon, the Chaldean, who destroyed this house, and carried the people away into Babylon. <hi type="super">13</hi> But in the first year of Cyrus the king of Babylon <hi type="italic">the same</hi> king Cyrus made a decree to build this house of God. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the vessels also of gold and silver of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took out of the temple that <hi type="italic">was</hi> in Jerusalem, and brought them into the temple of Babylon, those did Cyrus the king take out of the temple of Babylon, and they were delivered unto <hi type="italic">one,</hi> whose name <hi type="italic">was</hi> Sheshbazzar, whom he had made governor; <hi type="super">15</hi> And said unto him, Take these vessels, go, carry them into the temple that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Jerusalem, and let the house of God be builded in his place. <hi type="super">16</hi> Then came the same Sheshbazzar, <hi type="italic">and</hi> laid the foundation of the house of God which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Jerusalem: and since that time even until now hath it been in building, and <hi type="italic">yet</hi> it is not finished. <hi type="super">17</hi> Now therefore, if <hi type="italic">it seem</hi> good to the king, let there be search made in the king's treasure house, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> there at Babylon, whether it be <hi type="italic">so,</hi> that a decree was made of Cyrus the king to build this house of God at Jerusalem, and let the king send his pleasure to us concerning this matter. <div eID="gen8609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8610" type="x-p"/> We have here, I. The cognizance which their neighbours soon took of the reviving of this good work. A jealous eye, it seems, they had upon them, and no sooner did the Spirit of God stir up the friends of the temple to appear for it than the evil spirit stirred up its enemies to appear against it. While the people built and ceiled their own houses their enemies gave them no molestation (<reference osisRef="Hag.1.4">Hag. i. 4</reference>), though the king's order was to put a stop to the building of the city (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.21">ch. iv. 21</reference>); but when they fell to work again at the temple then the alarm was taken, and all heads were at work to hinder them, <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.3-Ezra.5.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. The adversaries are here named: <hi type="italic">Tatnai</hi> and <hi type="italic">Shethar-boznai.</hi> The governors we read of (<reference osisRef="Ezra.4.1-Ezra.4.24">ch. iv.</reference>) were, it is probable, displaced at the beginning of this reign, as is usual. It is the policy of princes often to change their deputies, proconsuls, and rulers of provinces. These, though real enemies to the building of the temple, were men of better temper than the other, and made some conscience of telling truth. If <hi type="italic">all men have not faith</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Thess.3.2">2 Thess. iii. 2</reference>), it is well some have, and a sense of honour. The church's enemies are not all equally wicked and unreasonable. The historian begins to relate what passed between the builders and those inquisitors (<reference osisRef="Ezra.5.3-Ezra.5.4">v. 3, 4</reference>), but breaks off his account, and refers to the ensuing copy of the letter they sent to the king, where the same appears more fully and at large, which he began to abridge (<reference osisRef="Ezra.5.4">v. 4</reference>), or make an extract out of, though, upon second thoughts, he inserted the whole. <div eID="gen8610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8611" type="x-p"/> II. The care which the divine Providence took of this good work (<reference osisRef="Ezra.5.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">The eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews,</hi> who were active in the work, so that their enemies could not cause them to cease, as they would have done, till the matter came to Darius. They desired they would only cease till they had instructions from the king about it. But they would not so much as yield them that, for <hi type="italic">the eye of God was upon them,</hi> even their God. And, 1. That baffled their enemies, infatuated and enfeebled them, and protected the builders from their malicious designs. While we are employed in God's work we are taken under his special protection; his eye is upon us for good, seven eyes upon one stone in his temple; see <reference osisRef="Zech.3.9">Zech. iii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.4.10">iv. 10</reference>. 2. That quickened them. The elders of the Jews saw <hi type="italic">the eye of God upon them,</hi> to observe what they did and own them in what they did well, and then they had courage enough to face their enemies and to go on vigorously with their work, notwithstanding all the opposition they met with. Our eye upon God, observing his eye upon us, will keep us to our duty and encourage us in it when the difficulties are ever so discouraging. <div eID="gen8611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8612" type="x-p"/> III. The account they sent to the king of this matter, in which we may observe, <div eID="gen8612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8613" type="x-p"/> 1. How fully the elders of the Jews gave the Samaritans an account of their proceedings. They, finding them both busy and prosperous, that all hands were at work to run up this building and that it went on rapidly, put these questions to them:—"By what authority do you do these things, and who gave you that authority? Who set you to work? Have you that which will bear you out?" To this they answered that they had sufficient warrant to do what they did; for, (1.) "<hi type="italic">We are the servants of the God of heaven and earth.</hi> The God we worship is not a local deity, and therefore we cannot be charged with making a faction, or setting up a sect, in building this temple to his honour: but we pay our homage to a God on whom the whole creation depends, and therefore ought to be protected and assisted by all and hindered by none." It is the wisdom as well as duty of kings to countenance the servants of the <hi type="italic">God of heaven.</hi> (2.) "We have a prescription to this house; it was built for the honour of our God by Solomon many ages ago. It is no novel invention of our own; we are but <hi type="italic">raising the foundations of many generations,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Isa. lviii. 12</reference>. (3.) "It was to punish us for our sins that we were, for a time, put out of the possession of this house; not because the gods of the nations had prevailed against our God, but because we had provoked him (<reference osisRef="Ezra.5.12">v. 12</reference>), for which he delivered us and our temple into the hands of the king of Babylon, but never intended thereby to put a final period to our religion. We were only suspended for a time, not deprived for ever." (4.) "We have the royal decree of Cyrus to justify us and bear us out in what we do. He not only permitted and allowed us, but charged and commanded us to build this house (<reference osisRef="Ezra.5.13">v. 13</reference>), and to build it in its place (<reference osisRef="Ezra.5.15">v. 15</reference>), the same place where it had stood before." He ordered this, not only in compassion to the Jews, but in veneration of their God, saying, <hi type="italic">He is the God.</hi> He also delivered the vessels of the temple to one whom he entrusted to see them restored to their ancient place and use, <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.14">v. 14</reference>. And they had these to show in confirmation of what they alleged. (5.) "The building was begun according to this order as soon as ever we had returned, so that we have not forfeited the benefit of the order for want of pursuing it in time; still it has been in building, but, because we have met with opposition, it is not finished." But, observe, they mention not the falsehood and malice of the former governors, nor make any complaint of them, though they had cause enough, to teach us not to render bitterness for bitterness, nor the most just reproach for that which is most unjust, but to think it enough if we can obtain fair treatment for the future, without an invidious reference to former injuries, <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.16">v. 16</reference>. This is the account they give of their proceedings, not asking what authority they had to examine them, nor upbraiding them with their idolatry, and superstitions, and medley religion. Let us learn hence with meekness and fear to <hi type="italic">give a reason of the hope that is in us</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.15">1 Pet. iii. 15</reference>), rightly to understand, and then readily to declare, what we do in God's service and why we do it. <div eID="gen8613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8614" type="x-p"/> 2. How fairly the Samaritans represented this to the king. (1.) They called the temple at Jerusalem the <hi type="italic">house of the great God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.5.8">v. 8</reference>); for though the Samaritans, as it should seem, had yet gods many and lords many, they owned the God of Israel to be the <hi type="italic">great God,</hi> who is above all gods. "It is the house of the <hi type="italic">great God,</hi> and therefore we dare not oppose the building of it without orders from thee." (2.) They told him truly what was done, not stating, as their predecessors did, that they were fortifying the city as if they intended war, but only that they were rearing the temple as those that intended worship, <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.8">v. 8</reference>. (3.) They fully represented their plea, told him what they had to say for themselves, and were willing that the cause should be set in a true light. (4.) They left it to the king to consult the records whether Cyrus had indeed made such a decree, and then to give directions as he should think fit, <reference osisRef="Ezra.5.17">v. 17</reference>. We have reason to think that if Artaxerxes, in the foregoing chapter, had had the Jews' cause as fairly represented to him as it was here to Darius, he would not have ordered the work to be hindered. God's people could not be persecuted if they were not belied, could not be baited if they were not dressed up in bears' skins. Let but the cause of God and truth be fairly stated, and fairly heard, and it will keep its ground.  <chapter eID="Ezra.5"/> <div eID="gen8614" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen8617" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8616" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Favourable Decree of Darius. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 519.)</title> <div sID="gen8618" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then Darius the king made a decree, and search was made in the house of the rolls, where the treasures were laid up in Babylon. <hi type="super">2</hi> And there was found at Achmetha, in the palace that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in the province of the Medes, a roll, and therein <hi type="italic">was</hi> a record thus written: <hi type="super">3</hi> In the first year of Cyrus the king <hi type="italic">the same</hi> Cyrus the king made a decree <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> the house of God at Jerusalem, Let the house be builded, the place where they offered sacrifices, and let the foundations thereof be strongly laid; the height thereof threescore cubits, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the breadth thereof threescore cubits;   4 <hi type="italic">With</hi> three rows of great stones, and a row of new timber: and let the expenses be given out of the king's house: <hi type="super">5</hi> And also let the golden and silver vessels of the house of God, which Nebuchadnezzar took forth out of the temple which <hi type="italic">is</hi> at Jerusalem, and brought unto Babylon, be restored, and brought again unto the temple which <hi type="italic">is</hi> at Jerusalem, <hi type="italic">every one</hi> to his place, and place <hi type="italic">them</hi> in the house of God. <hi type="super">6</hi> Now <hi type="italic">therefore,</hi> Tatnai, governor beyond the river, Shethar-boznai, and your companions the Apharsachites, which <hi type="italic">are</hi> beyond the river, be ye far from thence: <hi type="super">7</hi> Let the work of this house of God alone; let the governor of the Jews and the elders of the Jews build this house of God in his place. <hi type="super">8</hi> Moreover I make a decree what ye shall do to the elders of these Jews for the building of this house of God: that of the king's goods, <hi type="italic">even</hi> of the tribute beyond the river, forthwith expenses be given unto these men, that they be not hindered. <hi type="super">9</hi> And that which they have need of, both young bullocks, and rams, and lambs, for the burnt offerings of the God of heaven, wheat, salt, wine, and oil, according to the appointment of the priests which <hi type="italic">are</hi> at Jerusalem, let it be given them day by day without fail: <hi type="super">10</hi> That they may offer sacrifices of sweet savours unto the God of heaven, and pray for the life of the king, and of his sons. <hi type="super">11</hi> Also I have made a decree, that whosoever shall alter this word, let timber be pulled down from his house, and being set up, let him be hanged thereon; and let his house be made a dunghill for this. <hi type="super">12</hi> And the God that hath caused his name to dwell there destroy all kings and people, that shall put to their hand to alter <hi type="italic">and</hi> to destroy this house of God which <hi type="italic">is</hi> at Jerusalem. I Darius have made a decree; let it be done with speed. <div eID="gen8618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8619" type="x-p"/> We have here, I. The decree of Cyrus for the building of the temple repeated. To this the Samaritans referred because the Jews pleaded it, and perhaps hoped it would not be found, and then their plea would be over-ruled and a stop put to their work. Search was ordered to be made for it among the records; for, it seems, the tribes had not taken care to provide themselves with an authentic copy of it, which might have stood them in good stead, but they must appeal to the original. It was looked for in Babylon (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.1">v. 1</reference>), where Cyrus was when he signed it. But, when it was not found there, Darius did not make that a pretence to conclude that therefore there was no such decree, and thereupon to give judgment against the Jews; but it is probable, having himself heard that such a decree was certainly made, he ordered the rolls in other places to be searched, and at length it was found at Achmetha, in the province of the Medes, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.2">v. 2</reference>. Perhaps some that durst not destroy it, yet hid it there, out of ill will to the Jews, that they might lose the benefit of it. But Providence so ordered that it came to light; and it is here inserted, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.3-Ezra.6.5">v. 3-5</reference>. 1. Here is a warrant for the building of the temple: <hi type="italic">Let the house of God at Jerusalem,</hi> yea, <hi type="italic">let that house be built</hi> (so it may be read), within such and such dimensions, and with such and such materials. 2. A warrant for the taking of the expenses of the building out of the king's revenue, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.4">v. 4</reference>. We do not find that they had received what was here ordered them, the face of things at court being soon changed. 3. A warrant for the restoring of the vessels and utensils of the temple, which Nebuchadnezzar had taken away (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.5">v. 5</reference>), with an order that the priests, the Lord's ministers, should return them all to their places in the house of God. <div eID="gen8619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8620" type="x-p"/> II. The confirmation of it by a decree of Darius, grounded upon it and in pursuance of it. <div eID="gen8620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8621" type="x-p"/> 1. The decree of Darius is very explicit and satisfactory. <div eID="gen8621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8622" type="x-p"/> (1.) He forbids his officers to do any thing in opposition to the building of the temple. The manner of expression intimates that he knew they had a mind to hinder it: <hi type="italic">Be you far hence</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.6">v. 6</reference>); <hi type="italic">let the work of this house of God alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.7">v. 7</reference>. Thus was the wrath of the enemy <hi type="italic">made to praise God</hi> and the remainder thereof did he restrain. <div eID="gen8622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8623" type="x-p"/> (2.) He orders them out of his own revenue to assist the builders with money, [1.] For carrying on the building, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.8">v. 8</reference>. Herein he pursues the example of Cyrus, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.4">v. 4</reference>. [2.] For maintaining the sacrifices there when it was built, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.9">v. 9</reference>. He ordered that they should be supplied with every thing they wanted both for burnt-offerings and meat-offerings. He was content it should be a rent-charge upon his revenue, and ordered it to be paid every day, and this without fail, that they might offer sacrifices and prayers with them (for the patriarchs, when they offered sacrifice, <hi type="italic">called on the name of the Lord,</hi> so did Samuel, Elijah, and others) for the life (that is, the happiness and prosperity) of the king and his sons, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.10">v. 10</reference>. See here how he gives honour, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To Israel's God, whom he calls once and again the <hi type="italic">God of heaven. Secondly,</hi> To his ministers, in ordering his commissioners to give out supplies for the temple service at the appointment of the priests. Those that thought to control them must now be, in this matter, at their command. It was a new thing for God's priests to have such an interest in the public money. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> To prayer: <hi type="italic">That they may pray for the life of the king.</hi> He knew they were a praying people, and had heard that God was nigh to them in all that which they called upon him for. He was sensible he needed their prayers and might receive benefit by them, and was kind to them in order that he might have an interest in their prayers. It is the duty of God's people to pray for those that are in authority over them, not only for the good and gentle, but also for the forward; but they are particularly bound in gratitude to pray for their protectors and benefactors; and it is the wisdom of princes to desire their prayers, and to engage them. Let not the greatest princes despise the prayers of the meanest saints; it is desirable to have them for us, and dreadful to have them against us. <div eID="gen8623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8624" type="x-p"/> (3.) He enforces his decree with a penalty (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.11">v. 11</reference>): "Let none either oppose the work and service of the temple or withhold the supports granted to it by the crown upon pain of death. If any alter this decree, let him be (<hi type="italic">hanged before his own door</hi> as we say), hanged upon a beam of his own house, and, as an execrable man, <hi type="italic">let his house be made a dunghill.</hi>" <div eID="gen8624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8625" type="x-p"/> (4.) He entails a divine curse upon all those kings and people that should ever have any hand in the destruction of this house, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.12">v. 12</reference>. What he would not do himself for the protection of the temple he desired that God, <hi type="italic">to whom vengeance belongs,</hi> would do. This bespeaks him zealous in the cause; and though this temple was, at length, most justly destroyed by the righteous hand of God, yet perhaps the Romans, who were the instruments of that destruction, felt the effects of this curse, for that empire sensibly declined ever after. <div eID="gen8625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8626" type="x-p"/> 2. From all this we learn, (1.) That the heart of kings is in the hand of God, and he turns it which way soever he pleases; what they are he makes them to be, for he is <hi type="italic">King of kings.</hi> (2.) That when God's time has come for the accomplishing of his gracious purposes concerning his church he will raise up instruments to promote them from whom such good service was not expected. <hi type="italic">The earth sometimes helps the woman</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.16">Rev. xii. 16</reference>), and those are made use of for the defence of religion who have little religion themselves. (3.) That what is intended for the prejudice of the church has often, by the overruling providence of God, been made serviceable to it, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.12">Phil. i. 12</reference>. The enemies of the Jews, in appealing to Darius, hoped to get an order to suppress them, but, instead of that, they got an order to supply them. Thus <hi type="italic">out of the eater comes forth meat.</hi> The apocryphal Esdras (or Ezra), <hi type="underline">Book I. ch. iii. and iv.</hi>, gives another account of this decree in favour of the Jews, that Darius had vowed that if ever he came to the kingdom he would build the temple at Jerusalem, and that Zerubbabel, who was one of his attendants (whereas it is plain here that he was now at Jerusalem), for making an ingenious discourse before him on that subject (<hi type="italic">Great is the truth and will prevail</hi>), was told to ask what recompence he would, and asked only for this order, in pursuance of the king's vow.

<div eID="gen8626" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Completion of the Second Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 516.)</title> <div sID="gen8627" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> Then Tatnai, governor on this side the river, Shethar-boznai, and their companions, according to that which Darius the king had sent, so they did speedily. <hi type="super">14</hi> And the elders of the Jews builded, and they prospered through the prophesying of Haggai the prophet and Zechariah the son of Iddo. And they builded, and finished <hi type="italic">it,</hi> according to the commandment of the God of Israel, and according to the commandment of Cyrus, and Darius, and Artaxerxes king of Persia. <hi type="super">15</hi> And this house was finished on the third day of the month Adar, which was in the sixth year of the reign of Darius the king. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the children of Israel, the priests, and the Levites, and the rest of the children of the captivity, kept the dedication of this house of God with joy, <hi type="super">17</hi> And offered at the dedication of this house of God an hundred bullocks, two hundred rams, four hundred lambs; and for a sin offering for all Israel, twelve he goats, according to the number of the tribes of Israel. <hi type="super">18</hi> And they set the priests in their divisions, and the Levites in their courses, for the service of God, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> at Jerusalem; as it is written in the book of Moses. <hi type="super">19</hi> And the children of the captivity kept the passover upon the fourteenth <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the first month. <hi type="super">20</hi> For the priests and the Levites were purified together, all of them <hi type="italic">were</hi> pure, and killed the passover for all the children of the captivity, and for their brethren the priests, and for themselves. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the children of Israel, which were come again out of captivity, and all such as had separated themselves unto them from the filthiness of the heathen of the land, to seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel, did eat, <hi type="super">22</hi> And kept the feast of unleavened bread seven days with joy: for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> had made them joyful, and turned the heart of the king of Assyria unto them, to strengthen their hands in the work of the house of God, the God of Israel. <div eID="gen8627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8628" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. The Jews' enemies made their friends. When they received this order from the king they came with as much haste to encourage and assist the work as their predecessors had done to put a stop to it, <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.23">ch. iv. 23</reference>. What the king ordered they did, and, because they would not be thought to do it with reluctance, they <hi type="italic">did it speedily,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.13">v. 13</reference>. The king's moderation made them, contrary to their own inclination, moderate too. <div eID="gen8628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8629" type="x-p"/> II. The building of the temple carried on, and finished in a little time, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.14-Ezra.6.15">v. 14, 15</reference>. Now the <hi type="italic">elders of the Jews built</hi> with cheerfulness. For aught I know, the elders themselves laboured at it <hi type="italic">with their own hands;</hi> and, if they did, it was no disparagement to their eldership, but an encouragement to the other workmen. 1. They found themselves bound to it <hi type="italic">by the commandment of the God of Israel,</hi> who had given them power that they might use it in his service. 2. They found themselves shamed into it by the commandment of the heathen kings, Cyrus formerly, Darius now, and Artaxerxes some time after. Can the elders of the Jews be remiss in this good work when these foreign princes appear so warm in it? Shall native Israelites grudge their pains and care about this building when strangers grudge not to be at the expense of it? 3. They found themselves encouraged in it by the prophesying of Haggai and Zechariah, who, it is likely, represented to them (as bishop Patrick suggests) the wonderful goodness of God in inclining the heart of the king of Persia to favour them thus. And now the work went on so prosperously that, in four years' time, it was brought to perfection. <hi type="italic">As for God, his work is perfect.</hi> The gospel church, that spiritual temple, is long in the building, but it will be finished at last, when the mystical body is completed. Every believer is a <hi type="italic">living temple, building up himself in his most holy faith.</hi> Much opposition is given to this work by Satan and our own corruptions. We trifle, and proceed in it with many stops and pauses; but he that has <hi type="italic">begun the good work</hi> will see it performed, and will <hi type="italic">bring forth judgment unto victory. Spirits of just men</hi> will be <hi type="italic">made perfect.</hi> <div eID="gen8629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8630" type="x-p"/> III. The dedication of the temple. When it was built, being designed only for sacred uses, <hi type="italic">they showed by an example how it should be used,</hi> which (says bishop Patrick) is the proper sense of the word <hi type="italic">dedicate.</hi> They entered upon it with solemnity and probably with a public declaration of the separating of it from common uses and the surrender of it to the honour of God, to be employed in his worship. 1. The persons employed in this service were not only <hi type="italic">the priests and Levites</hi> who officiated, but <hi type="italic">the children of Israel,</hi> some of each of the <hi type="italic">twelve tribes,</hi> though Judah and Benjamin were the chief, and <hi type="italic">the rest of the children of the captivity</hi> or <hi type="italic">transportation,</hi> which intimates that there were many besides the children of Israel, of other nations, who transported themselves with them, and became proselytes to their religion, unless we read it, <hi type="italic">even the remnant of the children of the captivity,</hi> and then, we may suppose, notice is hereby taken of their mean and afflicted condition, because the consideration of that helped to make them devout and serious in this and other religious exercises. A sad change! The <hi type="italic">children of Israel</hi> have become <hi type="italic">children of the captivity,</hi> and there appears but a remnant of <hi type="italic">them,</hi> according to that prediction (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.3">Isa. vii. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">Shear-jashub—The remnant shall return.</hi> 2. The sacrifices that were offered upon this occasion were <hi type="italic">bullocks, rams, and lambs</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.17">v. 17</reference>), for burnt-offerings and peace-offerings; not to be compared, in number, with what had been offered at the dedication of Solomon's temple, but, being according to their present ability, they were accepted, for, <hi type="italic">after a great trial of affliction, the abundance of their joy, and their deep poverty, abounded to the riches of their liberality,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.2">2 Cor. viii. 2</reference>. These hundreds were more to them than Solomon's thousands were to him. But, besides these, they offered twelve he-goats for sin-offerings, one for every tribe, to make atonement for their sins, which they looked upon as necessary in order to the acceptance of their services. Thus, by getting iniquity taken away, they would free themselves from that which had been the sting of their late troubles, and which, if not removed, would be a worm at the root of their present comforts. 3. This service was performed with joy. They were all glad to see the temple built and the concerns of it in so good a posture. Let us learn to welcome holy ordinances with joy and attend on them with pleasure. Let us serve the Lord with gladness. Whatever we dedicate to God, let it be done with joy that he will please to accept of it. 4. When they dedicated the house they settled the household. Small comfort could they have in the temple without the temple service, and therefore they <hi type="italic">set the priests in their divisions</hi> and <hi type="italic">the Levites in their courses,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.18">v. 18</reference>. Though the temple service could not now be performed with so much pomp and plenty as formerly, because of their poverty, yet perhaps it was performed with as much purity and close adherence to the divine institution as ever, which was the true glory of it. No beauty like the beauty of holiness. <div eID="gen8630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8631" type="x-p"/> IV. The celebration of the passover in the newly-erected temple. Now that they were newly delivered out of their bondage in Babylon it was seasonable to commemorate their deliverance out of their bondage in Egypt. Fresh mercies should put us in mind of former mercies. We may suppose that they had kept the passover, after a sort, every year since their return, for they had an altar and a tabernacle. But they were liable to frequent disturbances from their enemies, were straitened for room, and had not conveniences about them, so that they could not do it with due solemnity till the temple was built; and now they made a joyful festival of it, it falling out in the next month after the temple was finished and dedicated, <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.19">v. 19</reference>. But now it is observed, to their praise, that <hi type="italic">they were purified together, as one man</hi> (so the word is); they were unanimous both in their resolutions and in their endeavours to make and keep themselves ceremonially clean for this solemnity; they joined together in their preparations, that they might help one another, so that all of them were pure, to a man. Of the proselytes that communicated with them in this ordinance: <hi type="italic">All such as had separated themselves unto them,</hi> had left their country and the superstitions of it and cast in their lot with the Israel of God, and had <hi type="italic">turned from the filthiness of the heathen of the land,</hi> both their idolatries and immoralities, <hi type="italic">to seek the Lord God of Israel</hi> as their God, did eat the passover. See how the proselytes, the converts, are described. They separated themselves from the filthiness of sin and fellowship with sinners, joined themselves with the Israel of God in conformity and communion, and set themselves to seek the God of Israel; and those that do so in sincerity, though strangers and foreigners, are welcome to eat of the gospel feast, as <hi type="italic">fellow-citizens with the saints and of the household of God.</hi> 3. Of the great pleasure and satisfaction wherewith they <hi type="italic">kept the feast of unleavened bread,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.6.22">v. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">The Lord had made them joyful,</hi> had given them both cause to rejoice and hearts to rejoice. It was now about twenty years since the foundation of this temple was laid, and we may suppose the old men that then wept at the remembrance of the first temple were most of them dead by this time, so that now there were no tears mingled with their joys. Those that are, upon good grounds, joyful, have therefore reason to be thankful, because it is God that <hi type="italic">makes them to rejoice.</hi> He is the fountain whence all the streams of our joy flow. God has promised to all those who take hold of his covenant that <hi type="italic">he will make them joyful in his house of prayer.</hi> The particular occasion they had for joy at this time was that God had <hi type="italic">turned the heart</hi> of the emperor to them, to <hi type="italic">strengthen their hands.</hi> If those that have been, or who we feared would have been, against us, prove to be for us, we may rejoice in it as a token for good, that <hi type="italic">our ways please the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.16.7">Prov. xvi. 7</reference>), and he must have the glory of it.  <chapter eID="Ezra.6"/> <div eID="gen8631" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen8634" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8633" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Ezra's Arrival at Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 457.)</title> <div sID="gen8635" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now after these things, in the reign of Artaxerxes king of Persia, Ezra the son of Seraiah, the son of Azariah, the son of Hilkiah, <hi type="super">2</hi> The son of Shallum, the son of Zadok, the son of Ahitub, <hi type="super">3</hi> The son of Amariah, the son of Azariah, the son of Meraioth, <hi type="super">4</hi> The son of Zerahiah, the son of Uzzi, the son of Bukki, <hi type="super">5</hi> The son of Abishua, the son of Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the chief priest: <hi type="super">6</hi> This Ezra went up from Babylon; and he <hi type="italic">was</hi> a ready scribe in the law of Moses, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel had given: and the king granted him all his request, according to the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> his God upon him. <hi type="super">7</hi> And there went up <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the children of Israel, and of the priests, and the Levites, and the singers, and the porters, and the Nethinims, unto Jerusalem, in the seventh year of Artaxerxes the king. <hi type="super">8</hi> And he came to Jerusalem in the fifth month, which <hi type="italic">was</hi> in the seventh year of the king. <hi type="super">9</hi> For upon the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the first month began he to go up from Babylon, and on the first <hi type="italic">day</hi> of the fifth month came he to Jerusalem, according to the good hand of his God upon him. <hi type="super">10</hi> For Ezra had prepared his heart to seek the law of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and to do <hi type="italic">it,</hi> and to teach in Israel statutes and judgments. <div eID="gen8635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8636" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. Ezra's pedigree. He was one of the sons of Aaron, a priest. Him God chose to be an instrument of good to Israel, that he might put honour upon the priesthood, the glory of which had been much eclipsed by the captivity. He is said to be <hi type="italic">the son of Seraiah,</hi> that Seraiah, as is supposed, whom the king of Babylon put to death when he sacked Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.18">2 Kings xxv. 18</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.21">21</reference>. If we take the shortest computation, it was seventy-five years since Seraiah died; many reckon it much longer, and, because they suppose Ezra called out in the prime of his time to public service, do therefore think that Seraiah was not his immediate parent, but his grandfather or great-grandfather, but that he was the first eminent person that occurred in his genealogy upwards, which is carried up here as high as Aaron, yet leaving out many for brevity-sake, which may be supplied from <reference osisRef="1Chr.6.4-1Chr.6.81">1 Chron. vi. 4</reference>, &c. He was a younger brother, or his father was Jozadak, the father of Jeshua, so that he was not high priest, but nearly allied to the high priest. <div eID="gen8636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8637" type="x-p"/> II. His character. Though of the younger house, his personal qualifications made him very eminent. 1. He was a man of great learning, a scribe, a <hi type="italic">ready scribe, in the law of Moses,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.6">v. 6</reference>. He was very much conversant with the scriptures, especially the writings of Moses, had the words ready and was well acquainted with the sense and meaning of them. It is to be feared that learning ran low among the Jews in Babylon; but Ezra was instrumental to revive it. The Jews say that he collected and collated all the copies of the law he could find out, and published an accurate edition of it, with all the prophetical books, historical and poetical, that were given by divine inspiration, and so made up the canon of the Old Testament, with the addition of the prophecies and histories of his own time. If he was raised up of God, and qualified and inclined to do this, all generations have reason to call him blessed, and to bless God for him. God sent to the Jews <hi type="italic">prophets and scribes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.34">Matt. xxiii. 34</reference>. Ezra went under the latter denomination. Now that prophecy was about to cease it was time to promote scripture-knowledge, pursuant to the counsel of God by the last of the prophets, <reference osisRef="Mal.4.4">Mal. iv. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Remember the law of Moses.</hi> Gospel ministers are called <hi type="italic">scribes instructed to the kingdom of heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.52">Matt. xiii. 52</reference>), New-Testament scribes. It was a pity that such a worthy name as this should be worn, as it was in the degenerate ages of the Jewish church, by men who were professed enemies to Christ and his gospel (<hi type="italic">Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees</hi>), who were learned in the letter of the law, but strangers to the spirit of it. 2. He was a man of great piety and holy zeal (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">He had prepared his heart to seek the law of the Lord,</hi> &c. (1.) That which he chose for his study was <hi type="italic">the law of the Lord.</hi> The Chaldeans, among whom he was born and bred, were famed for literature, especially the study of the stars, to which, being a studious man, we may suppose that Ezra was tempted to apply himself. But he got over the temptation; the law of his God was more to him than all the writings of their magicians and astrologers, which he knew enough of with good reason to despise them. (2.) He <hi type="italic">sought the law of the Lord,</hi> that is, he made it his business to enquire into it, searched the scriptures, and sought the knowledge of God, of his mind and will, in the scriptures, which is to be found there, but not without seeking. (3.) He made conscience of doing according to it; he set it before him as his rule, formed his sentiments and temper by it, and managed himself in his whole conversation according to it. This use we must make of our knowledge of the scriptures; for happy are we if we do what we know of the will of God. (4.) He set himself <hi type="italic">to teach Israel the statutes and judgments</hi> of that law. What he knew he was willing to communicate for the good of others; for <hi type="italic">the ministration of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal.</hi> But observe the method: he first learned and then taught, sought the law of the Lord and so laid up a good treasure, and then instructed others and laid out what he had laid up. He also first did and then taught, practised the commandments himself and then directed others in the practice of them; thus his example confirmed his doctrine. (5.) He <hi type="italic">prepared his heart</hi> to do all this, or he fixed his heart. He took pains in his studies, and thoroughly furnished himself for what he designed, and then put on resolution to proceed and persevere in them, and thus he became a ready scribe. Moses in Egypt, Ezra in Babylon, and both in captivity, were wonderfully fitted for eminent services to the church. <div eID="gen8637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8638" type="x-p"/> III. His expedition to Jerusalem for the good of his country: <hi type="italic">He went up from Babylon</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.6">v. 6</reference>), and, in four months' time, came to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.8">v. 8</reference>. It was strange that such a man as he staid so long in Babylon after his brethren had gone up; but God sent him not thither till he had work for him to do there; and none went but those <hi type="italic">whose spirits God raised</hi> to go up. Some think that this Artaxerxes was the same with that Darius whose decree we had (<reference osisRef="Ezra.6.1-Ezra.6.12">ch. vi.</reference>), and that Ezra came the very year after the temple was finished: that was the sixth year, this the seventh (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.8">v. 8</reference>), so Dr. Lightfoot. My worthy and learned friend, lately deceased, Mr. Talents, in his chronological tables, places it about fifty-seven years after the finishing of the temple; others further on. I have only to observe, 1. How kind the king was to him. He <hi type="italic">granted him all his request,</hi> whatever he desired to put him into a capacity to serve his country. 2. How kind his people were to him. When he went many more went with him, because they desired not to stay in Babylon when he had gone thence, and because they would venture to dwell in Jerusalem when he had gone thither. 3. How kind his God was to him. He obtained this favour from his king and country by <hi type="italic">the good hand of the Lord that was upon him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.6">v. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.9">9</reference>. Note, Every creature is that to us which God makes it to be, and from him our judgment proceeds. As we must see the events that <hi type="italic">shall</hi> occur in the hand of God, so we must see the hand of God in the events that <hi type="italic">do</hi> occur, and acknowledge him with thankfulness when we have reason to call it his <hi type="italic">good hand.</hi>

<div eID="gen8638" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Decree of Artaxerxes. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 457.)</title> <div sID="gen8639" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">11</hi> Now this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the copy of the letter that the king Artaxerxes gave unto Ezra the priest, the scribe, <hi type="italic">even</hi> a scribe of the words of the commandments of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and of his statutes to Israel. <hi type="super">12</hi> Artaxerxes, king of kings, unto Ezra the priest, a scribe of the law of the God of heaven, perfect <hi type="italic">peace,</hi> and at such a time. <hi type="super">13</hi> I make a decree, that all they of the people of Israel, and <hi type="italic">of</hi> his priests and Levites, in my realm, which are minded of their own freewill to go up to Jerusalem, go with thee. <hi type="super">14</hi> Forasmuch as thou art sent of the king, and of his seven counsellors, to enquire concerning Judah and Jerusalem, according to the law of thy God which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in thine hand; <hi type="super">15</hi> And to carry the silver and gold, which the king and his counsellors have freely offered unto the God of Israel, whose habitation <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Jerusalem, <hi type="super">16</hi> And all the silver and gold that thou canst find in all the province of Babylon, with the freewill offering of the people, and of the priests, offering willingly for the house of their God which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Jerusalem: <hi type="super">17</hi> That thou mayest buy speedily with this money bullocks, rams, lambs, with their meat offerings and their drink offerings, and offer them upon the altar of the house of your God which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Jerusalem. <hi type="super">18</hi> And whatsoever shall seem good to thee, and to thy brethren, to do with the rest of the silver and the gold, that do after the will of your God. <hi type="super">19</hi> The vessels also that are given thee for the service of the house of thy God, <hi type="italic">those</hi> deliver thou before the God of Jerusalem. <hi type="super">20</hi> And whatsoever more shall be needful for the house of thy God, which thou shalt have occasion to bestow, bestow <hi type="italic">it</hi> out of the king's treasure house. <hi type="super">21</hi> And I, <hi type="italic">even</hi> I Artaxerxes the king, do make a decree to all the treasurers which <hi type="italic">are</hi> beyond the river, that whatsoever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the God of heaven, shall require of you, it be done speedily, <hi type="super">22</hi> Unto a hundred talents of silver, and to a hundred measures of wheat, and to a hundred baths of wine, and to an hundred baths of oil, and salt without prescribing <hi type="italic">how much.</hi> <hi type="super">23</hi> Whatsoever is commanded by the God of heaven, let it be diligently done for the house of the God of heaven: for why should there be wrath against the realm of the king and his sons? <hi type="super">24</hi> Also we certify you, that touching any of the priests and Levites, singers, porters, Nethinims, or ministers of this house of God, it shall not be lawful to impose toll, tribute, or custom, upon them. <hi type="super">25</hi> And thou, Ezra, after the wisdom of thy God, that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in thine hand, set magistrates and judges, which may judge all the people that <hi type="italic">are</hi> beyond the river, all such as know the laws of thy God; and teach ye them that know <hi type="italic">them</hi> not. <hi type="super">26</hi> And whosoever will not do the law of thy God, and the law of the king, let judgment be executed speedily upon him, whether <hi type="italic">it be</hi> unto death, or to banishment, or to confiscation of goods, or to imprisonment. <div eID="gen8639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8640" type="x-p"/> We have here the commission which the Persian emperor granted to Ezra, giving him authority to act for the good of the Jews; and it is very ample and full, and beyond what could have been expected. The commission runs, we suppose, in the usual form: <hi type="italic">Artaxerxes, King of kings.</hi> This however is too high a title for any mortal man to assume; he was indeed king of some kings, but to speak as if he were king of all kings was to usurp <hi type="italic">his</hi> prerogative who hath <hi type="italic">all power both in heaven and in earth.</hi> He sends greeting to his trusty and well-beloved Ezra, whom he calls a <hi type="italic">scribe of the law of the God of heaven</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.12">v. 12</reference>), a title which (it seems by this) Ezra valued himself by, and desired no other, no, not when he was advanced to the proconsular dignity. He reckoned it more his honour to be a <hi type="italic">scribe of God's law</hi> than to be a peer or prince of the empire. Let us observe the articles of this commission. <div eID="gen8640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8641" type="x-p"/> I. He gives Ezra leave to go up to Jerusalem, and as many of his countrymen as pleased to go up with him, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.13">v. 13</reference>. He and they were captives, and therefore they would not quit his dominions without his royal license. <div eID="gen8641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8642" type="x-p"/> II. He gives him authority to enquire into the affairs of Judah and Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.14">v. 14</reference>. The rule of his enquiry was to be <hi type="italic">the law of his God, which was in his hand.</hi> He must enquire whether the Jews, in their religion, had and did according to that law—whether the temple was built, the priesthood was settled, and the sacrifices were offered conformably to the divine appointment. If, upon enquiry, he found any thing amiss, he must see to get it amended, and, like Titus in Crete, must <hi type="italic">set in order the things that were wanting,</hi> <reference osisRef="Titus.1.5">Tit. i. 5</reference>. Thus is God's law magnified and made honourable, and thus are the Jews restored to their ancient privilege of governing themselves by that law, and are no longer under <hi type="italic">the statutes that were not good,</hi> the statutes of their oppressors, <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.25">Ezek. xx. 25</reference>. <div eID="gen8642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8643" type="x-p"/> III. He entrusts him with the money that was freely given by the king himself and his counsellors, and collected among his subjects, for the service of the house of God, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.15-Ezra.7.16">v. 15, 16</reference>. <div eID="gen8643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8644" type="x-p"/> 1. Let this be taken notice of, (1.) To the honour of God, as the one only living and true God;' for even those that worshipped other gods were so convinced of the sovereignty of the God of Israel that they were willing to incur expenses in order to recommend themselves to his favour. See <reference osisRef="Ps.45.12">Ps. xlv. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.26">lxviii. 26</reference>. (2.) To the praise of this heathen king, that he honoured the God of Israel though his worshippers were a despicable handful of poor men, who were not able to bear the charges of their own religion and were now his vassals, and that, though he was not wrought upon to quit his own superstitions, yet he protected and encouraged the Jews in their religion, and did not only say, <hi type="italic">Be you warmed, and be you filled,</hi> but gave them such things as they needed. (3.) To the reproach of the memory of the wicked kings of Judah. Those that had been trained up in the knowledge and worship of the <hi type="italic">God of Israel,</hi> and had his law and his prophets, often plundered and impoverished the temple; but here a heathen prince enriched it. Thus afterwards the gospel was rejected by the Jews, but welcomed by the Gentiles. See <reference osisRef="Rom.11.11">Rom. xi. 11</reference>, <hi type="italic">Through their fall salvation has come to the Gentiles.</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.13.46">Acts xiii. 46</reference>. <div eID="gen8644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8645" type="x-p"/> 2. We are here told that Ezra was entrusted, (1.) To receive this money and to carry it to Jerusalem; for he was a man of known integrity, whom they could confide in, that he would not convert to his own use the least part of that which was given to the public. We find Paul going to Jerusalem upon such an errand, <hi type="italic">to bring alms to his nation and offerings,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.24.17">Acts xxiv. 17</reference>. (2.) To lay out this money in the best manner, in sacrifices to be offered upon the altar of God (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.17">v. 17</reference>), and in whatever else he or his brethren thought fit (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.18">v. 18</reference>), with this limitation only that it should be <hi type="italic">after the will of their God,</hi> which they were better acquainted with than the king was. Let the <hi type="italic">will of our God</hi> be always our rule in our expenses, and particularly in what we lay out for his service. God's work must always be done according to his will. Besides money, he had vessels also given him for the service of the temple, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.19">v. 19</reference>. Cyrus restored what of right belonged to the temple, but these were given over and above: thus it <hi type="italic">receiveth its own with usury.</hi> These he must <hi type="italic">deliver before the God of Jerusalem,</hi> as intended for his honour, there where he had <hi type="italic">put his name.</hi> <div eID="gen8645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8646" type="x-p"/> IV. He draws him a bill, or warrant rather, upon the <hi type="italic">treasurers on that side the river,</hi> requiring them to furnish him with what he had occasion for out of the king's revenues, and to place it to the king's account, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.20">v. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.22">22</reference>. This was considerately done; for Ezra, having yet to enquire into the sate of things, knew not what he should have occasion for and was modest in his demand. It was also kindly done, and evinced a great affection to the temple and a great confidence in Ezra. It is the interest of princes and great men to use their wealth and power for the support and encouragement of religion. What else are great revenues good for but that they enable men to do much good of this kind if they have but hearts to do it? <div eID="gen8646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8647" type="x-p"/> V. He charges him to let nothing be wanting that was requisite to be done in or about the temple for the honour of the God of Israel. Observe, in this charge (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.23">v. 23</reference>), 1. How honourably he speaks of God. He had called him before <hi type="italic">the God of Jerusalem;</hi> but here, lest it should be thought that he looked upon him as a local deity, he calls him twice, with great veneration, the <hi type="italic">God of heaven.</hi> 2. How strictly he eyes the word and law of God, which, it is likely, he had read and admired: "Whatsoever is <hi type="italic">commanded by your God</hi>" (whose institutions, though he wrote himself <hi type="italic">King of kings,</hi> he would not presume in the least iota or tittle to alter or add to) "let it be done, let it be diligently done, with care and speed." And, 3. How solicitously he deprecates the wrath of God: <hi type="italic">Why should there be wrath against the realm?</hi> The neglect and contempt of religion bring the judgments of God upon kings and kingdoms; and the likeliest expedient to turn away his wrath, when it is ready to break out against a people, is to support and encourage religion. Would we secure our peace and prosperity? Let us take care that the cause of God be not starved. <div eID="gen8647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8648" type="x-p"/> VI. He exempts all the ministers of the temple from paying taxes to the government. From the greatest of the priests to the least of the Nethinim, <hi type="italic">it shall not be lawful</hi> for the king's officers <hi type="italic">to impose</hi> that <hi type="italic">toll, tribute, or custom upon them,</hi> which the rest of the king's subjects paid, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.24">v. 24</reference>. This put a great honour upon them as free denizens of the empire, and would gain them respect as favourites of the crown; and it gave them liberty to attend their ministry with more cheerfulness and freedom. We suppose it was only what they needed for themselves and their families, and the maintenance of their ministry, that was hereby allowed to come to them custom-free. If any of them should take occasion from this privilege to meddle in trade and merchandise, they justly lost the benefit of it. <div eID="gen8648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8649" type="x-p"/> VII. He empowers Ezra to nominate and appoint judges and magistrates for all the Jews on that side the river, <reference osisRef="Ezra.7.25-Ezra.7.26">v. 25, 26</reference>. It was a great favour to the Jews to have such nobles of themselves, and especially to have them of Ezra's nomination. 1. All that <hi type="italic">knew the laws of Ezra's God</hi> (that is, all that professed the Jewish religion) were to be under the jurisdiction of these judges, which intimates that they were exempted from the jurisdiction of the heathen magistrates. 2. These judges were allowed and encouraged to make proselytes: Let them <hi type="italic">teach the laws of God</hi> to <hi type="italic">those that do not know them.</hi> Though he would not turn Jew himself, he cared not how many of his subjects did. 3. They were authorized to enforce the judgments they gave, and the orders they made, conformable to <hi type="italic">the law of God</hi> (which was hereby made <hi type="italic">the law of the king</hi>), with severe penalties—imprisonment, banishment, fine, or death, according as their law directed. They were not allowed to make new laws, but must see the laws of God duly executed; and they were entrusted with the sword in order that they might be <hi type="italic">a terror to evil doers.</hi> What could Jehoshaphat, or Hezekiah, or David himself, as king, have done more for the honour of God and the furtherance of religion?

<div eID="gen8649" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Ezra's Thankfulness to God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 457.)</title> <div sID="gen8650" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">27</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of our fathers, which hath put <hi type="italic">such a thing</hi> as this in the king's heart, to beautify the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Jerusalem: <hi type="super">28</hi> And hath extended mercy unto me before the king, and his counsellors, and before all the king's mighty princes. And I was strengthened as the hand of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> my God <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon me, and I gathered together out of Israel chief men to go up with me. <div eID="gen8650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8651" type="x-p"/> Ezra cannot proceed in his story without inserting his thankful acknowledgement of the goodness of God to him and his people in this matter. As soon as he has concluded the king's commission, instead of subjoining, <hi type="italic">God save the king</hi> (though that would have been proper enough), he adds, <hi type="italic">Blessed be the Lord;</hi> for we must <hi type="italic">in every thing give thanks,</hi> and, whatever occurrences please us, we must own God's hand in them, and praise his name. Two things Ezra blessed God for:—1. For his commission. We suppose he kissed the king's hand for it, but that was not all: <hi type="italic">Blessed be God</hi> (says he) <hi type="italic">that put such a thing as this into the king's heart.</hi> God can put things into men's hearts which would not arise there of themselves, and into their heads too, both by his providence and by his grace, in things <hi type="italic">pertaining both to life and godliness.</hi> If any good appear to be in our own hearts, or in the hearts of others, we must own it was God that put it there, and bless him for it; for it is he that <hi type="italic">worketh in us both to will and to do</hi> that which is good. When princes and magistrates act for the suppression of vice, and the encouragement of religion, we must thank God that <hi type="italic">put it into their hearts</hi> to do so, as much as if they had granted us some particular favour. When God's house was built Ezra rejoiced in what was done to beautify it. We read not of any orders given to paint or gild it, or to garnish it with precious stones, but to be sure that the ordinances of God were administered there constantly, and carefully, and exactly according to the institution; and that was indeed the beautifying of the temple. 2. For the encouragement he had to act in pursuance of his commission (<reference osisRef="Ezra.7.28">v. 28</reference>): <hi type="italic">He has extended mercy to me.</hi> The king, in the honour he did him, we may suppose, had an eye to his merit, and preferred him because he looked upon him to be a very sensible ingenious man; but he himself ascribes his preferment purely to God's mercy. It was this that recommended him to the favour of his prince. Ezra himself was a man of courage, yet he attributed his encouragement not to his own heart, but to God's hand: "I was strengthened to undertake the services, <hi type="italic">as the hand of the Lord my God was upon me</hi> to direct and support me." If God gives us his hand, we are bold and cheerful; if he withdraws it, we are weak as water. Whatever service we are enabled to do for God and our generation, God must have all the glory of it. Strength for it is derived from him, and therefore the praise of it must be given to him.  <chapter eID="Ezra.7"/> <div eID="gen8651" type="x-p"/>

<div eID="gen8654" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8653" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Journey of Ezra and Others.
